1. Written foundations and the chapter contract

This chapter reconciles Stanford CS 221 Spring 2026 written CSP modules, Berkeley CS 188 textbook CSP material, CMU 15-281 Fall 2025 written notes, MIT 16.410 Fall 2010 constraint lectures by Brian Williams, and the relevant CSP slides of Cornell CS 4700 Fall 2013 by Bart Selman. Harvard CS 50 AI written CSP and crossword explanations provide an additional implementation comparison. The source audit records the bounded candidate pool, exact reading scopes, source errors, unavailable material and the reasons for selecting complementary contributions. A course index or successful download is not counted as actual course reading.

The mathematical core is a finite constraint satisfaction problem. Continuous optimization and arbitrary probabilistic inference are different problems. We introduce weighted factor graphs only after the feasibility problem is clear. The executable reference and laboratory cover finite binary relations; higher-arity/global constraints are taught with separate, explicitly identified models rather than silently passed to a binary solver. Prerequisites are finite sets, relations, elementary graphs, recursion, induction, products and asymptotic bounds. Each new notion is developed here before being used.

The learning target is to translate a statement into exact variables and constraints, distinguish local from global evidence, justify each pruning step, calculate a search or propagation bound under its assumptions, and explain why a completed answer follows. The chapter supplies difficult transfers and original-examination applications. Its finite sources and tests are not a guarantee about every unseen examination question.

2. Variables, domains, relations and solutions

A finite CSP has variables X1,…,Xn, finite domains D1,…,Dn, and constraints. A constraint has an ordered scope (Xi1,…,Xik) and an allowed relation R⊆Di1×…×Dik. Its arity is k. A complete assignment chooses one value for every variable. It is a solution exactly when its tuple on every scope lies in the corresponding relation. A domain is a set of allowable values; it is not a single chosen value.

For example, A,B,C∈{1,2,3} with A<B and B=C has solutions (1,2,2),(1,3,3),(2,3,3). The first relation is the three-pair table {(1,2),(1,3),(2,3)}; the second is equality. Listing three independent domains does not permit all 33 tuples after constraints are imposed. Conversely, repeated occurrences of the same variable name do not create additional independent choices.

A partial assignment fixes only some variables. In this chapter it is locally consistent when every fully instantiated constraint is satisfied. This is necessary, but not sufficient, for extension to a solution. A globally extendible partial assignment has at least one complete solution extension. Keeping those phrases separate prevents the common error of treating a locally legal search node as a promise of eventual success.

The empty assignment is a solution of an empty constraint system with no variables: the empty Cartesian product contains one empty tuple. A variable with an empty domain instead makes a CSP impossible, even if it has no incident edges. A false zero-arity constraint also makes a system impossible; such constants must be checked separately when an implementation supports them. The binary reference accepts explicit variable domains and binary constraints, not zero-arity or general higher-arity input.

3. Modeling changes the search space

In N -queens, use one variable Qi per row, with value equal to its column. For distinct rows i,j, impose Qi≠Qj and |Qi-Qj|≠|i-j|. Row occupancy is built into the representation. There are NN complete column tuples before testing attacks. For N=4, the two solutions are (2,4,1,3) and (3,1,4,2).

An alternative Boolean encoding uses N2 variables Bij∈{0,1}. At-most-one constraints alone admit the all-zero board. Exactly-one in each row, together with column/diagonal attack restrictions, supplies the missing occupancy requirement. The Boolean universe has 2N2 assignments; a larger universe does not by itself prove slower solving because propagation structure also changes.

For scheduling, an event-variable encoding gives each event one allowed time-slot value and imposes all-different on the event variables. A slot-variable encoding instead assigns an event or an empty marker to each slot and requires every event to occur exactly once. These are equivalent only after the missing occupancy, uniqueness and allowed-slot conditions are all included. Count variables, domain sizes, constraint arities and propagation strength; do not compare encodings only by one of those counts.

4. Constraint graphs and factor graphs

For a binary CSP, a constraint graph has one variable vertex per variable and an edge for each related pair. Unary restrictions can be absorbed into domains first. The edge means that the pair has a relation; it does not mean the relation is symmetric. The ordered table for A<B and the reversed table for testing B against A represent the same constraint viewed from opposite ends.

Several constraints on the same variable pair should be conjoined into one effective relation if the algorithm claims joint pair consistency. Equality and inequality separately both give supports on two identical two-element domains, but their conjunction allows no pair. Testing them separately with different witnesses is a weaker procedure and cannot justify the same deductions as testing their intersection.

A factor graph is bipartite: variable nodes connect to separate factor nodes naming their scopes. A three-variable parity constraint is one arity-three factor. Replacing it by an ordinary triangle of binary projections generally loses information. For even Boolean parity, every two-variable projection is the full binary relation, yet only four of the eight complete triples satisfy parity. The higher-arity relation cannot be recovered from those projections.

5. Why assignment order creates redundant paths

Suppose all n domains have size d, and temporarily ignore early constraint rejection. A search that chooses any unassigned variable and then a value has branching factors nd,(n-1)d,…,d. Its number of complete paths is n!dn. There are only dn different complete assignments: the extra factor counts all orders of writing the same choices.

Fixing which variable is selected at each node removes that permutation redundancy. The selector may depend on the current domains, as MRV does, provided it returns one unassigned variable and every value needed for completeness is eventually considered. For uniform domains and a fixed variable order, the full tree contains 1+d+…+dn nodes, not merely its dn leaves. For d>1 this sum is (dn+1-1)/(d-1); for d=1 it is n+1. Constraints can prune the tree but do not change this unconstrained counting argument.

The number of all distinct partial maps of arbitrary scope is instead ∑k=0n(nk)dk=(1+d)n. That set is different from the prefix states visited by one fixed-order tree. Distinguish complete assignments, partial assignments, action-order paths, expanded nodes and primitive relation checks whenever an examination asks for a count.

6. Backtracking: invariant, soundness and completeness

Backtracking maintains a locally consistent partial assignment. It chooses one unassigned variable, tries its values, rejects any value inconsistent with earlier choices, recurses and then restores the earlier state before trying a sibling. A complete candidate must satisfy every constraint, including higher-arity constraints whose last variable has just been assigned. A depth- n path supplies a full assignment; hitting a failed branch returns to the nearest choice point with another value available.

Soundness. A returned assignment uses domain values and has all variables fixed. Each constraint was checked when its scope became fully assigned, or is checked explicitly at return. Therefore every returned assignment satisfies the original CSP.

Completeness. Let s be a solution extending a current node. Whatever unassigned variable is selected, its value in s is among the values to be tried. Checking constraints against s cannot reject that value. Sound filtering cannot delete it either. Induct on the number of unassigned variables to obtain a path to s. If every branch fails, no solution exists below that node. For a finite CSP, finitely many choices ensure termination. A failure at the empty root disproves satisfiability; a failure below an assumption disproves only that branch.

Searching for one solution may stop at the first verified complete assignment. Counting all solutions must continue. Proving an optimum for weighted factors also cannot stop at an arbitrary feasible assignment. The stopping rule is part of the problem, not a cosmetic implementation detail.

7. MRV, degree and deterministic ties

Minimum remaining values chooses an unassigned variable with the smallest current legal domain. An empty domain is a failure certificate; a singleton is a forced remaining choice. MRV is a fail-first policy: every variable will eventually need a value, so exposing a difficult variable early can avoid exploring irrelevant later choices. It is a heuristic, not a theorem that runtime always improves.

The residual-degree tie-breaker prefers the tied variable constraining the largest number of other unassigned variables. Count distinct remaining neighbors, not two directed arcs per neighbor, already assigned neighbors or the variable's own domain size. On a fixed complete binary graph the initial degrees are equal, but later filtering can make MRV different. A low-degree singleton still wins under MRV-first ordering over a high-degree variable with several values.

To make a trace reproducible, state a complete rule: smallest current domain, then largest residual degree, then the declared variable order. State value tie-breaking separately. “Use MRV” alone may leave several valid traces when domains tie. If domains have not been maintained, counting their raw initial sizes can fail to measure the legal values remaining under the current assignment; either compute legal counts or explain the weaker heuristic actually used.

8. Least-constraining value is a declared score

After selecting X, one usual LCV score counts the neighbor-domain values that would be deleted by assigning X=a:

L(a)=∑Y∈N(X),Y unassigned|{b∈DY:(a,b)∉RXY}|.

Try smaller L(a) first. Since the pre-choice total neighbor-domain size is the same for every candidate, this is equivalent to maximizing the remaining number of individual neighbor values under the same one-step test. It is not equivalent to minimizing the number of affected neighboring variables. Deleting three values in one neighbor can be worse than deleting one in each of two neighbors.

A propagation-based LCV policy may trial-run AC -3 for each candidate and count the eventual domain loss. That is a different, more expensive score; restore domains after each trial. Neither score generally maximizes the exact number of complete solutions. With nonnegative weighted factors, a highly flexible feasible value can still have a worse objective. The heuristic's usefulness and its cost depend on whether the task is finding one solution, counting solutions or proving an optimum.

9. Forward checking and its precise boundary

After assigning X=a, restrict DX to {a}. For each unassigned neighbor Y, remove b∈DY if (b,a)∉RYX. Fail immediately if a neighbor loses every value. This is one layer of filtering from the new assignment; it does not normally propagate the resulting changes between two other unassigned variables.

For equality chain A=B=C with all domains {0,1}, assigning A=0 makes forward checking reduce B to {0} but leaves C unchanged. Further consistency propagation reduces C to {0} too. A singleton produced by filtering need not yet be recorded as an explicit search assignment; the algorithm can still select and assign it later. Domain state, assignment state and recursive depth are different records.

With maximum degree δ, largest domain d, a fixed head singleton and constant-time relation lookup, one such forward-checking pass uses O(δd) pair checks. A generic REVISE routine against an arbitrary head domain instead has O(d2) cost per arc. State which operation is being counted before quoting a coarse O(nd2) or a tighter bound.

10. Directed arc consistency and support witnesses

An arc X→Y is consistent when every surviving a∈DX has at least one surviving support b∈DY with (a,b)∈RXY. The quantifiers are for every tail value, there exists a head support. Different tail values may use different supports; a support need not itself extend to a global solution. Reverse consistency is a separate directed test.

For X+Y=4 with DX={1,2,3,4,5} and DY={1,2}, only X=2 and X=3 survive. Their supports are respectively Y=2 and Y=1. Values one, four and five have no head support. The operation deletes from DX only; it does not delete Y values merely because it was called in the forward direction.

For asymmetric relation X<Y, reversing the arc uses RYX={(b,a):(a,b)∈RXY}. It must not reinterpret the reverse test as a new requirement Y<X. A unary condition must be enforced before a claim of node-and-arc consistency. An isolated variable is not protected from an empty domain merely because there are no arcs to process.

11. REVISE and AC -3 queue discipline

REVISE snapshots the tail domain, checks each candidate against the current head domain and removes candidates having no support. Snapshotting avoids modifying a set or list while iterating over that same live container. If any tail value is deleted, neighboring variables may have lost a support in that changed domain. Enqueue existing incoming arcs Z→X, not outgoing arcs X→Z.

With one conjoined relation per unordered pair and the reverse relation stored as its transpose, rechecking Y→X immediately after revising X→Y is unnecessary. A removed a supported no current value of Y, so its removal cannot be the cause of a lost support in that reverse arc. If a program handles several separate constraints with different witnesses, this exclusion needs a fresh proof; the chapter's reference avoids that ambiguity by conjoining relations first.

Full preprocessing starts with all directed constraint arcs. After assigning a variable in a previously arc-consistent branch, it suffices to start with incoming arcs to that changed singleton, then propagate every resulting domain change. That incremental initialization is not sufficient for an arbitrary unprocessed CSP: some disconnected arc may already be inconsistent. Queue order changes the intermediate trace and primitive-check count; it does not license deleting a supported value.

12. Why propagation is sound and terminates

Solution-preservation invariant. Assume the current domains contain all values used by every solution compatible with the current branch assumptions. If REVISE deletes a from DX, no b in the current DY satisfies their relation. Any compatible complete solution using X=a would have to choose such a b, a contradiction. Therefore deletion preserves every compatible solution. Induction over the finite deletion sequence proves the invariant for AC -3 and for its use inside backtracking.

Termination. Values are only removed, never created, within one propagation invocation. There are at most ∑i|Di| possible deletions. Requeueing happens only after a strict shrink; every such event adds finitely many existing arcs. The queue therefore eventually empties or an empty domain is detected. Repeated unchanged revisions do not generate more work.

Fixed-point meaning. When the full queue finishes successfully, every required directed arc has current support for every tail value. An arc processed earlier could become invalid only after its head domain changed; that change would have requeued it. If execution stops early on a wipeout, the other displayed domains are merely that particular partial failure trace, not necessarily a unique fully propagated closure. Across fair complete closure runs, monotone support deletion has a greatest arc-consistent subdomain below the starting domains; arbitrary early-failure snapshots need not be identical.

13. Deriving the AC -3 time bound

Let e be the number of directed binary arcs after parallel constraints have been conjoined, and d≥1 the largest starting domain. A naive revision examines at most d tail values and up to d head candidates for each, so costs O(d2) relation tests with constant-time table lookup. An arc is initially queued once and can be requeued only when its head domain strictly shrinks. Before a domain becomes empty, it can strictly shrink at most d-1 times. On empty-domain detection this implementation returns before adding further arcs. Thus each arc can be processed at most d times under this declared queue contract.

Multiplying gives O(ed3) time for binary relation checks, plus domain initialization and representation costs. For a dense graph e=O(n2), yielding O(n2d3). A sparse graph should retain e rather than silently replacing it by n2. If a constraint evaluation itself costs c, multiply the pair-test cost by c. Initial empty-domain checks still require reading the variable list even when e=0.

The maintained state requires O(nd+e) space for domains and a deduplicated arc queue, excluding the input relation tables. Explicit binary tables may themselves require O(ed2) storage. Keeping every teaching snapshot or every solution adds separate output storage; it is not part of the lean solver's auxiliary-space bound. A bound for one AC -3 invocation is not the total cost across an exponential search tree.

14. Arc consistency does not decide general satisfiability

Take a triangle with two colors and inequality on all three edges. Every tail color has the other color as a support across each individual edge. AC -3 deletes nothing. Yet choosing A=0 forces B=1 and C=1, violating B≠C; choosing A=1 gives the symmetric contradiction. There is no complete solution. Nonempty arc-consistent domains are necessary local evidence, not a sufficient global certificate.

By contrast, an empty domain after sound propagation proves that no solution extends the current assumptions. At the root this disproves the original CSP. Under A=0 it disproves only that branch; another value of A may succeed. A successful propagation call therefore returns an arc-consistency status, not a verified solution, and a failed branch does not justify declaring every sibling impossible.

15. Maintaining arc consistency and restoring a branch

MAC combines complete backtracking with AC -3 after each assignment. The root is first made arc consistent. At a child, fix the selected variable to one value and start incremental propagation from incoming arcs. Continue only if no domain empties. MRV then uses the smaller current domains, which can change its next selection substantially.

Restoration is essential to the completeness proof. Copying all domains for each child is simple and safe: siblings never share a mutable filtered domain. A trail is more efficient when carefully implemented. Record each deletion with its variable and value, save a trail length at the branch entrance, and restore entries back to that marker when leaving the child. Also restore explicit assignments, cached supports or counts, and any queue state a particular implementation reuses. A cached support removed later must be revalidated before it is used again.

For X≤Y, Y=Z, X≠Z on Boolean domains, the branch X=1 fails: Y must be one and Z must be zero, contradicting equality. Restoring the original branch domains and trying X=0 succeeds with (0,1,1). Keeping the wiped domain from the first branch would wrongly reject this valid solution. A deletion justified under an assumption cannot be applied globally without that assumption or a logically valid learned constraint.

16. Executable finite binary reference

The following reference implements explicit binary relations, conjunction of repeated pair constraints, directed support tests, an initial empty-domain guard, deterministic MRV/degree ties and exact branch copying. It uses integers as teaching values. Every AC -3 snapshot records the domains, current arc, support witness or deletion reason and remaining queue. The validator compares this actual printed algorithm with independent enumeration of small CSPs; the finite comparison supplements the general proofs above.

The following complete reference uses integer-coded domains, one conjoined table per pair, explicit initial-domain guards and branch copies. Python hash tables give expected constant-cost membership; the asymptotic discussion separately states its lookup assumptions. The browser laboratory independently implements the same finite support semantics.

"""Finite binary CSP algorithms with explicit domains, queue direction and rollback."""
from collections import deque
from copy import deepcopy
from itertools import product

class CSP:
    def __init__(self, domains, constraints):
        self.variables=tuple(domains)
        if len(set(self.variables))!=len(self.variables):raise ValueError('Repeated variable')
        self.initial={v:list(values) for v,values in domains.items()}
        if any(not isinstance(v,str) or not v for v in self.variables):raise ValueError('Use nonempty string variable names')
        if any(type(a)is not int for values in self.initial.values() for a in values):raise ValueError('Teaching domains use integer values')
        if any(len(values)!=len(set(values)) for values in self.initial.values()):raise ValueError('Domains must contain distinct values')
        self.relations={};self.labels={};self.neighbors={v:[] for v in self.variables}
        for c in constraints:
            x,y=c['x'],c['y']
            if x not in domains or y not in domains or x==y:raise ValueError('Use distinct declared endpoints')
            allowed={tuple(p) for p in c['allowed']}
            if any(len(p)!=2 or p[0]not in domains[x]or p[1]not in domains[y]for p in allowed):raise ValueError('Relation tuple outside its original domains')
            if (x,y)in self.relations:allowed&=self.relations[x,y]
            self.relations[x,y]=allowed;self.relations[y,x]={(b,a)for a,b in allowed}
            self.labels[x,y]=c.get('label',x+' ~ '+y);self.labels[y,x]=self.labels[x,y]
        for x,y in self.relations:
            if y not in self.neighbors[x]:self.neighbors[x].append(y)
        for x in self.variables:self.neighbors[x].sort(key=self.variables.index)
    def arcs(self):
        return [(x,y)for x in self.variables for y in self.neighbors[x]]
    def valid(self,assignment):
        if any(x not in self.initial for x in assignment):return False
        return all(x not in assignment or assignment[x]in self.initial[x]for x in self.variables)and all(x not in assignment or y not in assignment or (assignment[x],assignment[y])in allowed for (x,y),allowed in self.relations.items())

def ac3(csp, domains=None, queue=None, record=True):
    """Mutate the supplied branch domains; True means arc consistency, not SAT."""
    D=deepcopy(csp.initial)if domains is None else domains
    Q=deque(dict.fromkeys(tuple(a)for a in(csp.arcs()if queue is None else queue)))
    queued=set(Q)
    if any((x,y)not in csp.relations for x,y in Q):raise ValueError('Queue contains a nonconstraint arc')
    events=[];checks=0
    def emit(kind,why,arc=None,removed=None,supports=None,before=None):
        if record:events.append({'kind':kind,'why':why,'arc':list(arc)if arc else None,'domains':deepcopy(D),'queue':[list(q)for q in Q],'removed':removed or[],'supports':supports or[],'before':before,'pairChecks':checks})
    emit('initial','Every displayed column is a variable domain. Queue entries are directed support tests.')
    if any(not D[v]for v in csp.variables):
        emit('failure','An initially empty domain is impossible, even when its variable is isolated.');return False,D,events
    while Q:
        x,y=Q.popleft();queued.remove((x,y));before=deepcopy(D)if record else None;allowed=csp.relations[x,y];removed=[];supports=[]
        for a in list(D[x]):
            witness=None
            for b in D[y]:
                checks+=1
                if (a,b)in allowed:witness=b;break
            supports.append({'tail':a,'head':witness})
            if witness is None:D[x].remove(a);removed.append(a)
        emit('revise','Inspect support in the head domain; delete only unsupported tail values.',(x,y),removed,supports,before)
        if removed:
            if not D[x]:emit('failure','This branch has no solution because its tail domain is empty.',(x,y));return False,D,events
            for z in csp.neighbors[x]:
                if z!=y and (z,x)not in queued:Q.append((z,x));queued.add((z,x))
            emit('requeue','A changed domain can invalidate supports in existing incoming neighboring arcs.',(x,y))
    emit('fixed-point','All queued support tests have stabilized. Nonempty arc-consistent domains alone do not prove satisfiability.')
    return True,D,events

def solve(csp, mode='mac', all_solutions=True):
    """Branch copying gives exact rollback; MRV, residual degree, then input order."""
    if mode not in ('plain','fc','mac'):raise ValueError('Unknown mode')
    answers=[]
    def visit(assignment,D):
        if any(not D[v]for v in csp.variables):return False
        if len(assignment)==len(csp.variables):
            if csp.valid(assignment):answers.append(dict(assignment));return not all_solutions
            return False
        remaining=[v for v in csp.variables if v not in assignment]
        x=min(remaining,key=lambda v:(len(D[v]),-sum(z not in assignment for z in csp.neighbors[v]),csp.variables.index(v)))
        for a in D[x]:
            branch=dict(assignment);branch[x]=a
            if not csp.valid(branch):continue
            child=deepcopy(D);child[x]=[a]
            if mode=='mac':ok,child,_=ac3(csp,child,[(z,x)for z in csp.neighbors[x]],False)
            elif mode=='fc':
                ok=True
                for z in csp.neighbors[x]:
                    if z in branch:continue
                    child[z]=[b for b in child[z]if (b,a)in csp.relations[z,x]]
                    if not child[z]:ok=False;break
            elif mode=='plain':ok=True
            else:raise ValueError('Unknown mode')
            if ok and visit(branch,child):return True
        return False
    D=deepcopy(csp.initial)
    if mode=='mac':
        ok,D,_=ac3(csp,D,record=False)
        if not ok:return answers
    visit({},D);return answers

def brute_force(csp):
    return [dict(zip(csp.variables,values))for values in product(*(csp.initial[v]for v in csp.variables))if csp.valid(dict(zip(csp.variables,values)))]

def relation(x,y,dx,dy,predicate,label=None):
    return {'x':x,'y':y,'allowed':[[a,b]for a in dx for b in dy if predicate(a,b)],'label':label or x+' ~ '+y}

def instance(domains,predicates):
    """Build an explicit finite relation table from declared mathematical rules."""
    return CSP(domains,[relation(x,y,domains[x],domains[y],f,label)for x,y,f,label in predicates])

Editable exact binary-relation laboratory

This is a teaching instrument, not a quiz. Supply at most six variables with at most five distinct integer values each, from −9 through 9. Enter explicit allowed pairs; restrictions already applied to one variable belong in its domain. Repeated declarations on a pair are conjoined. The solver reports local consistency or a failure certificate; it does not call nonempty AC domains a solution.

The full snapshot list is a teaching output and can be much larger than the solver state. Setting recording off avoids that trace storage. The browser laboratory independently executes the same binary contract on bounded inputs and is checked against exact Python results; it is not presented as a general solver for arbitrary global constraints or continuous domains.

17. Tree and forest CSPs: backward filtering, forward assignment

Assume a finite binary constraint graph is a tree and domains have already absorbed unary restrictions. Choose a root and order variables so each parent comes before its children. In reverse order, revise the parent domain against each child domain. If a domain empties, report failure. Otherwise choose any remaining root value, then walk forward assigning each child a value supporting its chosen parent value.

Why it works. After processing a child's entire subtree, every surviving child value extends to a valid assignment in that subtree, by induction from leaves upward. Parent revision retains only values supported by such a child value. Distinct child subtrees have no cross edges in a tree, so their extensions can be combined independently. Consequently every surviving root value extends to the whole tree. The forward pass selects those witnesses. This argument fails on a cycle because two “subtrees” may contain an additional linking constraint.

There are n-1 edges, each requiring at most d2 pair checks in the backward pass; the forward pass needs at most O(nd) witness work. Total time is O(nd2) with constant-time binary checks. A forest is handled component by component, including isolated nonempty-domain variables. Linear time in n means the domain bound and relation-check convention are fixed; it does not mean linear in every possible input representation.

18. Counting tree solutions with messages

Existence and counting are different tasks. Define Mi(a) as the number of valid assignments in the subtree rooted at Xi when Xi=a. For a leaf, Mi(a)=1 for every allowed value. For an internal node,

Mi(a)=∏j∈children(i)(∑b∈Dj:(a,b)∈RijMj(b)).

The inner sum counts the child's choices and their descendant extensions; the product combines independent child subtrees. The total is ∑a∈DrMr(a). For a forest, multiply component totals, not add them. The number of arithmetic operations has the same pairwise structure as tree solving, but integer bit complexity can grow with the solution count. This is not a claim that arbitrarily large exact integers cost constant time.

A three-variable path with three colors and inequality has 3·2·2=12 solutions. The existential tree algorithm returns one; the message calculation counts all twelve. A root value with two different supported child values contributes both to the sum, rather than requiring one support shared across all root choices.

19. Cycle cutsets and the assumptions hidden in a bound

A cycle cutset is a set of variables whose removal leaves a forest. Given a cutset of size c, enumerate its at most dc assignments, reject those violating constraints internal to the cutset, restrict residual domains against the assigned boundary and solve each remaining forest. If any branch succeeds, combine its cutset assignment and forest assignment into a full solution.

The familiar O(dc(n-c)d2) expression describes the residual forest work under additional simplifications. It must not erase internal/boundary checking or give zero work when c=n. A safe binary-operation accounting for a supplied cutset is O(dc(e+nd2)) when checks are constant time, with room to sharpen sparse cases. Searching for a minimum cutset is a separate combinatorial task and is not included in that supplied-cutset bound. A larger known cutset may still be useful; minimality is not needed for correctness.

For a triangle with three colors, condition on one vertex. Each of its three choices leaves two adjacent vertices with two colors; the edge permits two completions. Total solution count is six. Conditioning does not make every cutset assignment feasible; each residual branch still needs its domain and edge checks.

20. Higher-arity constraints, global support and Hall reasoning

Pairwise inequalities and the global all-different relation have the same complete solutions, but their propagation strength can differ. Let DX=DY={1,2} and DZ={1,2,3}. Pairwise inequality is arc consistent without deleting one or two from DZ. Global all-different requires X,Y to use the two-value set {1,2}, leaving Z=3.

The underlying counting principle is Hall's condition: any subset of variables must collectively have at least as many possible values as variables if distinct values are to be assigned. Three variables all restricted to {1,2} violate that condition, although each binary inequality still has local support. A global support test for a candidate value must find a single satisfying tuple for the entire relation containing that value. Different pairwise witnesses are insufficient.

An explicit hidden-tuple encoding can convert a finite arity- k relation to binary constraints. Add an auxiliary variable whose domain is the set of allowed k -tuples; connect it to each original variable with a projection-equality relation. Every original solution has a corresponding tuple value and every satisfying extended assignment projects to an original solution. The encoding is exact, but the tuple domain can have up to dk entries. “Everything can be made binary” is not a promise of small memory or identical propagation behavior.

21. Path consistency, k-consistency and strong consistency

A CSP is k -consistent when every consistent assignment to any k-1 distinct variables extends to any selected k th variable. The one-variable extension condition requires an allowed value for every selected variable. Unary filtering is often called node consistency, but merely checking that every surviving value satisfies unary restrictions can be vacuously true on an empty domain. For the construction theorem below, require a nonempty unary-consistent base explicitly. Binary arc consistency then corresponds to the two-variable extension condition in this binary model. Three-consistency requires extension of an already compatible pair, a stronger question than finding independent supports on two edges.

Strong k -consistency means consistency at every level from one through k. Strong n -consistency permits a backtrack-free construction in any variable order: extend a consistent prefix of length zero, one, and so on by the appropriate next-level condition. The distinction is important: merely finding at least one solution on every k -variable subset does not establish the universal extension quantifier in the definition.

Path consistency can remove an allowed pair (a,b)∈RXY when some third variable Z has no value jointly supporting that pair through both relevant relations. In the Boolean triangle X=Y, Y=Z, X≠Z, every binary arc has support but no allowed X,Y pair extends through Z. Pair-relation filtering exposes the contradiction. Relation tables may need to be introduced or expanded as a stronger-consistency algorithm operates; the extra cost is part of the algorithm and its representation.

22. Conflicts, backjumping and legitimate learning

Chronological backtracking returns to the immediately preceding assigned variable. Conflict-directed reasoning asks which earlier assumptions actually caused failure. Suppose X4=X1 and X4=1, while X2,X3 are unrelated choices. Under X1=0, no value for X4 works. Changing only X2 or X3 cannot fix that contradiction, so returning directly to X1 is justified. Its explanation is the incompatible assumptions on X1 and X4, not merely the fact that X4 happened to be assigned last.

A conflict set records earlier variables whose current assignments suffice for the rejection. When every value of a variable fails, combine the explanations needed to reject all those values; a reason for only one value does not justify eliminating every value. Jump to the most recent relevant earlier assignment and retain the necessary earlier causes when propagating the explanation upward. The implementation must define how reasons from propagation and prior failures are accumulated; a static graph neighbor list is not automatically a complete dynamic explanation.

A nogood is a partial assignment proved not to have any solution extension. Its negation can be retained as a logically implied constraint. A branch-specific deleted value without its antecedent is not a global nogood. Learning is sound only when every retained clause or relation follows from the original constraints and recorded assumptions. The MIT notes identify omitted protected pseudocode; this chapter teaches the reasoning and a checked example, without pretending the removed text was available or presenting a full conflict-directed solver as part of the binary laboratory.

23. Complete-assignment repair and min-conflicts

Local search begins with a complete assignment and changes values to reduce violations, rather than extending an empty assignment. One min-conflicts policy selects a currently conflicting variable, computes how many constraints would be violated under each of its values and tries a minimum-scoring value. Count violated constraints or attacking queen pairs as declared; that is different from the number of variables participating in at least one violation.

This can work extremely well on some instances, but a positive conflict score is not an unsatisfiability certificate. The method can plateau, cycle under equal-score moves or become trapped in a local minimum. A finite iteration budget and unsuccessful restarts do not establish that no solution exists. The triangle with two colors has minimum conflict count one, but that lower bound follows from the parity argument, not merely from one unsuccessful run.

If an implementation accepts only strictly improving moves in a finite state space, it terminates because the objective has finitely many values. It can still terminate at a non-solution. If equal-value moves are allowed, a tie policy or separate stopping rule is needed; finite assignments alone do not prevent cycling. A complete backtracking search and an incomplete repair procedure have different failure meanings.

24. Weighted factors, partial bounds and approximate search

For nonnegative factors fj, define W(x)=∏jfj(x). Ordinary hard constraints are the special case fj∈{0,1}. A zero factor vetoes a complete assignment; a positive weight states feasibility under the zero/nonzero interpretation but not optimality. Probabilities need additional normalization/interpretation and are not implied merely by multiplying nonnegative numbers.

When extending a partial assignment, multiply each newly fully instantiated factor exactly once. Its scope determines when it becomes evaluable. If remaining factors may exceed one, the current partial product is not an upper bound on future weight. A partial weight two can later become twenty after a factor ten. A valid crude maximization upper bound is the current product times an upper bound for every unevaluated factor, with bounds taken over all remaining permitted values. Shared variables can make the product loose, but looseness does not invalidate an upper bound.

Beam search keeps at most K surviving partial assignments per depth. It can discard the unique feasible or optimal completion and is generally incomplete. With n levels, at most d extensions per candidate, constant incremental scoring and linear-time top- K selection, the work is O(nKd). Sorting instead adds a logarithmic selection factor; randomized quickselect provides expected linear selection, not an unqualified deterministic worst-case guarantee. Copying whole assignments or evaluating many factors adds its own cost. A fixed beam size does not establish a universal approximation ratio.

Coordinate-wise maximization of weighted factors is another incomplete local method. If unaffected factors are strictly positive, their common multiplicative constant can be omitted when comparing a single-coordinate move. If that constant is zero, all full products remain zero and the local comparison cannot claim a strict global improvement. Keep a current value on ties or define a full-sweep stopping policy when proving convergence; arbitrary equal-weight moves may cycle.

25. A complete examination decision sequence

First identify whether the question concerns feasibility, counting, optimization or one particular algorithm trace. Write the actual domains, unary restrictions, relation scopes and any branch assumptions. Draw a binary graph only for binary constraints; give higher-arity constraints their own representation. If a graph comes from a map, use the exact adjacencies, not a guessed geographic picture.

For a propagation question, write every directed queue entry in its stated order. For a popped arc, list tail values and at least one valid head witness for each survivor. Delete only unsupported tail values. Record incoming requeues after a strict shrink, stop under the specified wipeout rule and distinguish intermediate from fixed-point domains. State whether the conclusion concerns the root or an assumed branch.

For heuristic questions, recompute current legal-domain sizes, apply MRV before a declared degree tie, count only residual neighbors and calculate the actual LCV score requested. Separate a variable-selection heuristic from a value-ordering heuristic. For a counting question, distinguish paths, distinct assignments, leaves, nodes, revisions and individual relation tests.

For a tree or cutset question, prove the structural assumption, check empty domains, identify supplied versus computed cutsets and account for boundary/internal constraints. For all-different or stronger-consistency questions, ask whether the same joint tuple supports all requirements, rather than assembling incompatible pairwise witnesses. Finally verify any returned full assignment against every original constraint. A local success flag, one positive factor or a plausible-looking coloring is not that final verification.

26. Fully worked mathematical and conceptual questions

IC 01 · Count assignments, paths and nodes separately

Original examination-style problem; reconciles the Stanford/CMU/Cornell assignment-order discussion.

Five variables have domains of size three and no constraints. Count complete assignments, complete paths when each action may select any unassigned variable, all distinct partial assignments, and nodes in a full fixed-order tree. Explain the different answers.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

A complete assignment chooses one of three values independently for each of five named variables, so there are 35=243. If actions may choose the next variable too, every complete assignment can be written in 5!=120 orders. The action tree therefore has 5!35=29160 complete paths, although many paths end at the same assignment.

For a distinct partial map, each variable is either unassigned or takes one of three values: four independent possibilities. Thus there are 45=1024 distinct partial maps, equivalently ∑k=05(5k)3k. A fixed variable order visits only prefix scopes, not every possible partial scope. Its complete tree has 1+3+9+27+81+243=364 nodes, of which 243 are leaves. None of these numbers counts primitive constraint tests because there are no constraints here. Early pruning would reduce the action tree, whereas merging equivalent states addresses a different source of redundancy. The source notation nd is not the count for n variables of domain size d.

IC 02 · Four queens and a nonadjacent-column relation

Adapted from MIT 16.410 Lecture 5, PDF page 13, with an independently derived complete solution.

Let Qi be the row of the queen in column i on a four-by-four board. Give the allowed relation between Q1 and Q3, then find every complete solution. Contrast the initial assignment count with a sixteen-variable Boolean encoding.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

The two columns are distance two apart. A pair (a,b) is allowed exactly when a≠b and |a-b|≠2. Enumerating the four possibilities for each coordinate leaves

R13={(1,2),(1,4),(2,1),(2,3),(3,2),(3,4),(4,1),(4,3)}.

Every complete solution must also satisfy the other five column-pair restrictions. Starting with Q1=1 leaves no complete nonattacking arrangement; Q1=2 forces the completion (2,4,1,3). Reflecting rows gives (3,1,4,2) from Q1=3; Q1=4 mirrors the failed first case. Independent enumeration of all 44=256 column tuples confirms exactly those two. Each uses distinct rows, and its six absolute row differences avoid the corresponding column differences.

The Boolean encoding starts with 216=65536 truth assignments before imposing occupancy and attack constraints. It must require exactly one queen per column or an equivalent total/occupancy condition. At-most-one attack constraints alone admit the empty board. The different universe sizes do not, by themselves, establish solver runtime.

IC 03 · Show a support for every surviving value

Adapted from Stanford CS 221 Spring 2026, Arc Consistency, written numerical example.

For X+Y=4, DX={1,2,3,4,5} and DY={1,2}, revise X→Y and then the reverse arc. List supports and the complete solutions.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Test tail candidates individually. For X=1, the required support is three, which is absent from DY; delete one. For X=2, support Y=2 exists. For X=3, support Y=1 exists. For X=4 and five, required supports zero and minus one are absent; delete both. Thus the first revision leaves DX={2,3} and does not itself alter DY.

On the reverse arc, Y=1 has support X=3 and Y=2 has support X=2. Neither is deleted, so the pair is arc consistent in both directions. The only complete solutions are (2,2) and (3,1). The surviving witnesses are different; arc consistency never requires one single Y value to support every X value simultaneously. In this two-variable example the surviving pairs characterize solutions exactly. That conclusion does not transfer to a general cyclic graph with several constraints. The displayed player records the direction, support witnesses and deleted tail values at each checkpoint.

IC 04 · Strict inequalities propagate from both ends

Original problem.

Variables A,B,C initially have domain {1,2,3,4} with A<B<C. Find the AC closure and every solution. Explain why just applying each inequality once may be insufficient.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

On A<B, value four has no larger support, so A loses four; B loses one because it has no smaller support. On B<C, B loses four and C loses one and two once B has minimum two. The loss of B=4 then removes support for A=3. The fixed point is DA={1,2}, DB={2,3}, DC={3,4}. Each survivor has a witness on each incident directed arc.

Complete solutions are the increasing triples (1,2,3),(1,2,4),(1,3,4),(2,3,4), one for each choice of three distinct values from four. Thus there are (43)=4, rather than the product 2·2·2=8 of the final domain sizes. Those domains record individually possible values, not unconstrained combinations. The path structure permits backtrack-free construction after directional filtering, but arbitrary independent selection from all final domains can still violate an edge. Requeueing is needed because a head-domain loss can invalidate an earlier tail support.

IC 05 · An extensional relation with holes

Adapted from Cornell CS 4700 Fall 2013, PDF page 76.

Let DX={1,2,3}, DY={3,4,5,6} and RXY={(1,3),(1,5),(3,3),(3,6)}. Find the arc-consistent domains and count complete solutions. Does a domain product give that count?

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Tail value X=2 appears in no allowed pair and is removed. Values one and three retain supports three/five and three/six respectively. Reversing the relation, Y=4 occurs in no allowed pair and is removed; Y=3,5,6 retain supports. The fixed-point domains are {1,3} and {3,5,6}.

The four listed allowed tuples are exactly the four complete solutions. The domain product has six tuples, including forbidden (1,6) and (3,5), so multiplying final domain sizes overcounts. Both domains may be nonempty and both directions supported while not every cross-product pair is compatible. The input is an extensional table, so a constant-time hashed-pair membership lookup supports the usual REVISE complexity assumption. Scanning the entire relation afresh for each pair would be a different implementation with an additional lookup cost. Keeping holes in a domain also matters: the surviving set is not the numeric interval from its minimum to its maximum.

IC 06 · A source triangle solved entirely by propagation

Adapted from MIT 16.410 Lecture 5, PDF pages 20–34.

Three variables are pairwise unequal. Their domains are D1={R,G,B}, D2={R,G} and D3={G}. Derive the closure and verify the complete assignment without guessing colors.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Because X3 can only be green, X2=G has no support on X2→X3 and is deleted, leaving X2=R. Likewise X1=G has no support against X3 and is removed. Now X1=R loses its only possible unequal support in D2, because that domain has become the singleton red. Hence D1={B}.

The remaining domains are ({B},{R},{G}). Check the three original inequalities: blue differs from red, blue differs from green and red differs from green. Thus the complete assignment (B,R,G) satisfies every constraint. It is unique because every variable's domain is a singleton and sound propagation preserved every solution. A different initial arc queue can display the deletions in a different order; a fair run still reaches this successful closure. The player uses integer color codes with an explicit legend, so a colored node never hides the actual declared domain value.

IC 07 · A locally supported but impossible triangle

Course-derived counterexample compared across Stanford, Cornell and Harvard written CSP discussions.

A triangle has inequality on every edge and Boolean domains. Prove it is arc consistent and unsatisfiable. Explain what MAC does after assigning its first variable.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

For either tail value zero or one, the opposite head value supports inequality across each edge. Therefore both directions of all three edges pass REVISE, and preprocessing removes nothing. This is a direct verification of the universal-tail/existential-head condition, not an inference from equal domain sizes.

For global impossibility, choose A=0. Inequality forces both B=1 and C=1, violating their mutual edge. Choosing A=1 gives the complementary failure. These two cases exhaust the first variable's domain, so there is no solution. Under MAC, either first assignment propagates to the two other singletons and then produces a wipeout. Each wipeout is initially a branch failure; after both first-variable branches have been exhausted, root failure establishes unsatisfiability. An isolated AC call returning nonempty domains has proved only local support. The contradiction is the inability to combine the separate witnesses into one joint coloring.

IC 08 · An even cycle with the same local domains

Original comparison problem.

Replace the previous triangle by a four-cycle A-B-C-D-A, still with two colors and inequality. Find its AC closure and its number of solutions. Why can the same local test coexist with a different satisfiability answer?

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Every directed edge again has opposite-color support for both values, so no domain changes. The final domains therefore look exactly like the triangle's initial/final domains when viewed one vertex at a time.

Choose A=0. The cycle forces B=1, C=0, D=1, and the closing edge D≠A is satisfied. Choosing A=1 gives the complementary coloring. Every remaining value is then forced along the path, so there are precisely two solutions, (0,1,0,1) and (1,0,1,0); no others can occur. An even number of inequality flips returns to the original color, whereas the triangle's odd number creates a contradiction. Arc consistency checks each pair separately and does not record that parity around the whole cycle. It is therefore consistent for AC to give identical domain sizes in the two problems while one has zero complete solutions and the other has two.

IC 09 · One layer versus propagated equality

Original problem.

In the equality chain A=B=C with Boolean domains, assign A=0. Compare forward checking with MAC. Count extensions of that branch.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Forward checking tests the arcs entering the newly assigned singleton A. Only B is its neighbor, so it deletes B=1 and leaves DB={0}. There is no direct A,C constraint, so a one-layer pass leaves DC={0,1}. That remaining one at C is not promised to extend to a solution; it has simply not been tested against the changed B domain.

MAC requeues C→B after B shrinks. Candidate C=1 now has no equal head support and is removed, leaving all three domains singleton zero. The branch has exactly one complete extension, (0,0,0), verified against both equalities. Before assigning A, the original CSP had two solutions, the all-zero and all-one assignments. The stronger pruning did not remove a valid branch extension; it exposed a consequence earlier. It also did not automatically increase recursive assignment depth: a solver can keep B,C as unassigned singleton-domain variables until it explicitly selects them.

IC 10 · Restore a failed branch before trying its sibling

Original hard implementation/correctness problem.

Boolean variables satisfy X≤Y, Y=Z and X≠Z. Try X=1 first and then X=0 with MAC. Show why sharing the failed domains across siblings is incorrect.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

In the first branch, X=1 and X≤Y force Y=1. The inequality X≠Z forces Z=0. Equality Y=Z then has no allowed pair, so propagation empties a domain and this branch fails. That failure used the assumption X=1.

Restore the parent domains DX=DY=DZ={0,1} before selecting X=0. Now X≠Z forces Z=1, equality forces Y=1, and 0≤1 is valid. Thus (0,1,1) is a complete solution. It is the only solution: X=1 was impossible, and X=0 forces the other two values as shown.

If a mutable domain emptied in the first branch is reused for the second without restoration, the solver rejects the valid solution and becomes incomplete. Branch copying avoids aliasing; a trail must restore every deletion back to its saved marker. The valid learned statement here is that X=1 has no extension, not that the emptied variable has no values under every possible assumption.

IC 11 · MRV first, residual degree second

Original examination-style heuristic problem.

Six variables remain unassigned. Their graph edges are AB, AC, BC, BE, CE and CF; D is isolated. Current domain sizes are |DA|=2, |DB|=2, |DC|=3, |DD|=1, |DE|=|DF|=4. Verify the residual degrees of A,B,C,D are two, three, four and zero. Use MRV, then maximum residual degree, then alphabetical order. Choose the next variable; after D is assigned without altering other domains, choose the next one.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

The smallest domain size is one, achieved only by D. It is selected despite having degree zero. The degree rule is a tie-breaker after MRV, not a license to override a strictly smaller domain. Selecting C because its degree is four would apply a different heuristic.

After assigning the isolated D, it is excluded from the candidate list. By the question's premise no other domain or residual degree changes. The new minimum domain size is two, tied between A and B. Of those, B has larger residual degree, three versus two, so it is selected. Alphabetical order is never reached in either decision. If a trace did not specify how MRV ties are broken, both A and B could be valid next choices under MRV alone. Current domain sizes, residual degrees and the sequence of priorities are all necessary to reproduce a deterministic trace.

IC 12 · Deleted values and affected neighbors rank differently

Original hard LCV counterexample.

Let X∈{a,b} and Y,Z∈{1,2,3,4}. Choosing a permits only Y=1 and permits every Z. Choosing b permits Y,Z∈{2,3,4}. No other constraints exist. Compare deleted-value LCV, affected-neighbor count and exact completion counts.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Under a, Y loses three values and Z loses none, so the deleted-value score is three. Under b, each neighbor loses one value, so the score is two. Standard one-step deleted-value LCV therefore prefers b. Equivalently the surviving individual value totals are 1+4=5 versus 3+3=6.

An affected-neighbor score instead counts one changed neighbor for a and two for b, so it prefers the opposite candidate. This demonstrates that the two definitions cannot be silently substituted. Exact completion counts are 1·4=4 for a and 3·3=9 for b, because the two neighbors have no linking constraint. In this instance LCV agrees with the larger solution count, but that agreement is not a general theorem once neighbors interact. Both candidates remain feasible, and the full CSP has thirteen solutions. The laboratory represents a,b by declared integer codes, preserving the actual allowed-pair tables.

IC 13 · Separate supports can contradict one another

Original consistency-definition problem.

On Boolean domains, impose both X=Y and X≠Y. Compare testing each relation separately with testing their conjunction. What must a solver do before using a one-relation-per-pair AC -3 proof?

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Equality supplies support Y=x for each value x of X; inequality supplies support Y=1-x. The same observations hold in reverse. Thus each separate binary relation is arc consistent on the unchanged full domains. However no pair can satisfy both relations, because equality and inequality are mutually exclusive.

Their effective joint relation is the intersection of the equality table {(0,0),(1,1)} and the inequality table {(0,1),(1,0)}, which is empty. Revising against that joint relation deletes both tail values and detects impossibility. Different witnesses for different predicates do not form one witness satisfying the conjunction. Before applying the chapter's exclusion of the just-revised reverse arc or its joint-support interpretation, conjoin all constraints on that pair, or otherwise explicitly enforce a consistency definition that uses a common witness. The complete solution set is empty in either representation, but the propagation strengths differ until the representation/algorithm is made precise.

IC 14 · Reverse the table, not the mathematical inequality

Original problem.

With X,Y∈{1,2,3} and X<Y, compute both directed revisions. Explain the error in checking Y<X on the reverse arc.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

The allowed forward pairs are (1,2),(1,3),(2,3). The forward arc deletes X=3, because no larger Y is available, and retains X values one and two. For the reverse test, use the transposed pairs (2,1),(3,1),(3,2) in Y,X order. It deletes Y=1, since no smaller X exists; Y values two and three survive. The final domains are DX={1,2} and DY={2,3}, with the same three complete solutions as the original relation table.

Checking the new condition Y<X would impose a different constraint rather than view the original from the other endpoint. Conjoining both strict inequalities would make the problem impossible. A directed arc describes which domain is being filtered and which supplies supports; it does not change the underlying admissible assignments. This distinction matters especially for inequalities, sums with asymmetric coefficients and scheduling precedences, even though it is easy to overlook on symmetric inequality/coloring examples.

IC 15 · A complete queue trace has a declared order

Original exact-trace problem.

For A<B<C on {1,2,3}, use initial FIFO queue (A,B),(B,A),(B,C),(C,B), append incoming affected arcs not already queued and omit the just-processed reverse. List domain changes and the fixed point.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

First (A,B) removes three from A, leaving A={1,2}. Next (B,A) removes one from B, leaving B={2,3}; its affected incoming arc (C,B) is already queued. Processing (B,C) removes B=3, leaving B={2}. This requeues (A,B) because A may have lost its support B=3. The original queued (C,B) now sees B={2} and removes C=1 and C=2, leaving C={3}. No additional incoming neighbor other than the just-processed B is present. Finally the requeued (A,B) deletes A=2, leaving A={1}.

The resulting singleton assignment is (1,2,3), and all edges are satisfied. The declared deduplicated queue processes five arcs; it performs more individual pair-membership checks than revisions. Reversing the initial queue would change intermediate deletions and possibly primitive-test counts. A correct final-domain answer cannot justify an invented intermediate queue trace; both the initialization and reinsertion convention are part of the question.

IC 16 · Empty domains and the empty variable set

Original algorithm-boundary problem.

Explain what a robust solver should return for (a) one isolated variable with empty domain, (b) one isolated variable with three values, and (c) no variables and no constraints. Why is an empty AC -3 queue alone insufficient to decide among them?

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

In case (a), no value can be assigned to the variable, so the system has zero solutions. There are no arcs, but an explicit initial-domain guard must still reject it. An algorithm that returns success immediately from an empty queue would give a false satisfiability impression here.

In case (b), each of the three values independently supplies a complete solution, so there are three. The empty arc queue correctly means no binary support tests are required; it does not select a value or count solutions by itself. In case (c), the empty assignment satisfies every constraint vacuously, so there is exactly one solution, the empty tuple. That is the empty-product convention underlying recursive base cases, not zero solutions.

If a system permits a false zero-arity constraint, case (c) changes to impossible and that constant must be checked. The printed binary reference does not accept such a constraint as an edge. These endpoint cases test whether the implementation has confused “no pending pair test” with “a verified complete assignment exists.”

IC 17 · Charge reprocessing to the head domain

Original calculation based on the written AC -3 analyses.

A binary CSP has 120 directed arcs and maximum initial domain size ten. Use the chapter's one-copy initial queue, immediate wipeout return and constant-time pair lookup. Give a safe bound on revisions and pair tests in one invocation. Does this bound cover all backtracking nodes together?

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

A particular directed arc is present initially once. It is requeued only after its head domain strictly shrinks; before becoming empty a ten-value domain can shrink at most nine times. A shrink to empty terminates before adding another queue batch. Thus at most ten revisions of that directed arc are possible. Across 120 arcs, at most 120·10=1200 revisions occur.

Each naive revision inspects at most ten tail candidates and ten head candidates for each, giving at most one hundred pair checks. Consequently 1200·100=120000 is a safe coarse pair-test bound. Early supporting witnesses, smaller later domains, deduplication and skipped reverse arcs often reduce it. If “120 edges” meant undirected edges, there would be 240 directed arcs and the numerical bound would double.

This is one propagation invocation. Backtracking can restore domains and invoke propagation at many different search nodes, so summing work across the whole tree can still be exponential. The bound also excludes input construction and the cost of a nonconstant constraint oracle. Those costs cannot be hidden inside a claimed exact revision count.

IC 18 · Why MAC keeps every solution despite stronger pruning

Original proof problem.

Prove completeness of MAC with deterministic dynamic ordering and branch copies. Identify the step that fails if a heuristic discards a nonempty candidate value without a sound reason.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Fix a solution s and a search node whose explicit assignments agree with it. Initially s's unassigned values lie in the node's domains. The selector chooses one unassigned variable X, possibly based on the current domains; it need not follow a fixed global order. When its candidate s(X) is tried, the partial assignment remains locally legal because it agrees with a solution.

Sound AC -3 cannot delete any remaining value used by s: a deleted value would lack a head support, while s itself supplies the compatible head value. Therefore the corresponding child survives. Inducting on the number of unassigned variables constructs a path to s. Exact branch copies ensure that a failed sibling cannot contaminate that child's domains. Finiteness and eventually trying every candidate ensure the path is eventually visited.

If a heuristic deletes a candidate merely because its LCV score is poor or a beam is full, the step “s(X) is eventually tried” may fail. Such a procedure can be useful but is not the complete MAC algorithm proved here. Ordering changes when a solution is sought; unsound pruning changes which solutions are still reachable.

IC 19 · Tree existence and exact counting are different

Original tree-CSP problem.

A path A-B-C has three colors at each vertex and inequality on each edge. Give a backtrack-free construction and count all solutions using subtree messages.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Root the tree at A. Backward parent-to-child revision deletes nothing because every color has two unequal child supports. Choose any A color, then one of its two supporting B colors, then one of the two C colors unequal to that chosen B. This verifies all edges and requires no backtracking after the backward sweep.

For counting, each fixed C color has leaf message one. For a fixed B color, summing over its two permitted C colors gives message two. For a fixed A color, the two permitted B colors each contribute two, so its subtree count is four. Summing over A's three colors gives twelve complete solutions. The product 33=27 ignores constraints, while returning one forward assignment solves only existence.

The message sum uses alternative choices within a child subtree; products would be used across several independent children. The arithmetic-operation count is O(nd2) under naive pair tables, but an arbitrarily large exact count can have growing bit length. The tree premise is essential to both the independent-subtree combination and the backtrack-free guarantee.

IC 20 · A tree can be rejected in the backward pass

Original problem.

A star has center H with domain {1,2,3} and leaves U={1}, V={2}, W={3}. Every leaf must differ from H. Perform the backward tree sweep and explain why no forward assignment should be attempted.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Each leaf has only its displayed value. Revising H against U removes H=1, because equality to that singleton would violate the edge. Revising H against V removes H=2. Revising H against W removes H=3. The center domain is now empty, establishing that no value can satisfy all three required inequalities simultaneously.

Every deletion has its own direct witness failure; the contradiction is not based on counting four vertices or assuming a star is automatically satisfiable. Trees admit a polynomial decision/construction algorithm, not a guarantee that every domain specification has a solution. The backward sweep is the existence test. Only if all required domains, including the root domain, remain nonempty does the forward witness construction become valid. Here a forward pass cannot choose a root value, so it must return failure. Processing the leaves in another order changes which color disappears first but not the conclusion that all three are excluded.

IC 21 · Independent components multiply solution counts

Original problem.

A forest consists of edges A-B and C-D, with Boolean domains and inequality, plus an isolated variable E having three values. Count complete solutions and explain what happens if E's domain is empty instead.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

The first edge has two solutions, (0,1) and (1,0). Independently, the second has the same two possibilities. A complete solution chooses one assignment from each component and one of E's three values. There are therefore 2·2·3=12 solutions. Adding component counts would wrongly count alternatives among components rather than simultaneous choices for all variables.

The Cartesian-product decomposition is exact because no constraint connects different components. Conversely any full solution restricts to a valid solution in each component, so the product count neither misses nor duplicates assignments. If E has an empty domain, its component has zero solutions and the product is zero even though both edge components remain arc consistent and satisfiable. A solver must inspect isolated variables; they do not appear in an arc queue. For finding one solution, solve each component and combine the assignments; for counting, multiply the component totals and respect exact-integer costs.

IC 22 · Condition one triangle variable and solve a forest

Original cutset-conditioning problem.

A triangle has three colors at every vertex and pairwise inequality. Use cutset {A}, count all solutions and describe the work that is performed in each cutset branch.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Removing A leaves the edge B-C, a tree. There are three cutset assignments, one for each A color. For a fixed choice, boundary constraints remove that color from both residual domains. The two remaining colors must be different on B-C, yielding two ordered completions. Thus the total is 3·2=6 solutions.

For each branch, first verify the chosen cutset values against constraints whose scopes lie inside the cutset; here there is no such edge. Then propagate the boundary restrictions to B and C, revise the residual tree and choose or count its supported assignments. The original triangle was cyclic, so the tree proof applies only after conditioning and boundary pruning.

The calculation uses a supplied valid cutset; it does not include finding a minimum one. Assigning a cutset does not imply that the residual CSP will succeed, although all three branches happen to do so here. Each returned coloring must include A and satisfy its two incident original edges as well as the residual B-C edge.

IC 23 · A cutset does not make every branch feasible

Original hard graph/propagation problem.

The complete graph K4 has three-color domains and inequality on every edge. Explain why one removed vertex is not a cycle cutset, why two are, and why conditioning on any two still yields no solution.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Removing one vertex leaves K3, which contains a triangle and is not a forest. Removing two leaves one edge, a tree, so any pair of vertices is a valid cycle cutset. Enumerate its 32=9 assignments. The three equal-color assignments violate the edge internal to the cutset and must be rejected before residual solving.

For each of the six distinct-color cutset assignments, every residual vertex is adjacent to both assigned vertices and loses those two colors. Both residual domains become the same singleton third color. Their mutual edge then has no unequal pair, so the residual tree fails. Thus all nine branches are rejected and the original graph has no three-coloring.

Root AC -3 alone would delete nothing because every individual unequal edge has supports in the full three-color domains. Conditioning exposes stronger joint consequences under its assumptions. This example separates “the remainder is a tree” from “the remainder is satisfiable,” and shows why internal cutset edges and boundary edges must both be included in a complexity/correctness description.

IC 24 · The all-variable cutset exposes a missing cost

Original asymptotic-boundary problem.

A formula for supplied-cutset solving is quoted as O(dc(n-c)d2). Set c=n and explain why literal zero work is wrong. Give a bound that includes the missing tasks.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

If every variable belongs to the cutset, the residual graph is empty, so its tree-solving term is indeed zero. But the algorithm still has to examine up to dn cutset assignments and verify constraints among them. The zero residual term is not the total algorithm cost. The empty remaining graph contributes one empty completion to each already valid full cutset assignment, rather than removing the need to check that assignment.

A safe operation accounting for a supplied cutset is O(dc(e+nd2)) with constant-time binary checks. It includes per-branch constraint checking and a conservative residual/boundary allowance. For c=n, a sharper direct enumeration description is O(dn(n+e)) if constructing each candidate costs O(n) and checking all edges costs O(e). Representation and enumeration choices can sharpen this further, but not to zero.

Finding the cutset itself is a separate task and is absent from both supplied-cutset formulas. The lesson is to distinguish the cost of a subroutine on the residual problem from the cost of the surrounding enumeration and verification.

IC 25 · Global all-different removes a locally supported value

Original Hall-set problem, motivated by the written global-constraint discussions.

Let X,Y have domains {1,2} and Z have {1,2,3}. Compare pairwise inequality AC with global all-different support. Find all solutions.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Pairwise AC deletes nothing: for any value of one variable, each other neighbor separately has a different value available. In particular Z=1 has X=2 as a support and Y=2 as another separate support. Those two witnesses cannot be used simultaneously because X and Y must also differ.

Under the global relation, the two variables X,Y must occupy the two available values {1,2}. Their set is a Hall set with exactly two variables and two possible values. Z cannot use either of those values, so its only globally supported value is three. Then X,Y must be (1,2) or (2,1), giving exactly (1,2,3) and (2,1,3).

The complete solution set of the pairwise-inequality encoding is the same as the global relation's; the difference is propagation strength. Pairwise AC's surviving Z values one and two are locally supported but globally impossible. A single matching/tuple-support test can explain those removals, while the ordinary binary trace must not claim to perform that stronger global algorithm.

IC 26 · Detect a Hall violation that every pair misses

Original problem.

Three variables each have domain {1,2} and must all be different. Prove unsatisfiability, verify pairwise arc consistency and explain why a global support check can fail before any explicit assignment.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

The union of the three domains contains only two values. Assigning three pairwise distinct values would require an injection from a three-element variable set into a two-element value set, which is impossible by the pigeonhole principle. In Hall form, the three-variable subset has a value union of size two, violating the necessary inequality three ≤ two.

Nevertheless every pairwise inequality has support for both values: one is supported by two and two by one. Thus binary AC -3 leaves all domains unchanged. It has not made an arithmetic mistake; it enforced a weaker consistency notion. A global all-different propagator can ask whether a matching covers every variable in the variable–value bipartite graph. No such matching exists here, so it can reject the entire current branch without selecting one variable first.

The global conclusion comes from one jointly feasible distinct-value allocation, not separate matches for each edge. In a fixed diagram, distinguish a currently chosen partial matching from the existence of any full matching. Failure of one greedy matching attempt alone would not prove the Hall violation; the two-value counting argument does.

IC 27 · A binary encoding must retain the entire allowed tuple

Original higher-arity modeling problem.

Boolean variables X,Y,Z have even parity: X+Y+Z is even. Find the allowed tuples, show why pairwise projections lose the constraint and construct an exact hidden-variable binary encoding.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

The allowed triples are 000, 011, 101 and 110. Projecting onto any pair gives all four Boolean pairs: for every selected pair there is exactly one value of the third variable completing even parity. Hence the triangle of pairwise projected constraints permits all eight triples, including invalid 001. It is not an equivalent representation.

Introduce auxiliary variable H with four domain values, one for each allowed triple. Connect H to X, Y and Z by projection constraints requiring each original value to equal the corresponding coordinate of H's chosen tuple. Any even-parity assignment extends by its own tuple H. Conversely, satisfying those three binary constraints forces X,Y,Z to be exactly an allowed H tuple. This proves equivalence in both directions.

The extra variable has tuple-valued states, not four independent choices for each coordinate. For a general arity-k table, its domain can have up to dk tuples. The encoding is finite and exact, but its size and propagation behavior must be accounted for; reducing arity is not a universal compression theorem.

IC 28 · Bare n-consistency can be vacuously true

Original consistency-hierarchy counterexample.

Three singleton-domain variables A,B,C each have domain {0} and pairwise inequality. Is the system 3-consistent under the extension definition? Is it strongly 3-consistent or satisfiable?

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

There is no consistent assignment to any pair: the only pair (0,0) violates its inequality. The statement “every consistent assignment to two variables extends to the third” is therefore vacuously true, because there are no consistent two-variable assignments to test. Thus bare 3-consistency holds under that quantified definition.

The system is not 2-consistent. The consistent singleton assignment A=0 cannot be extended to B, since B's only value is equal to A. Consequently it is not strongly 3-consistent, which requires all lower consistency levels too. It is also unsatisfiable, directly from any one inequality edge.

This example explains why a backtrack-free theorem must include strong consistency and a usable nonempty unary-consistent base. Bare high-order extension statements may become true for the unhelpful reason that lower-order assignments already do not exist. Do not read a universal statement over an empty set as an existence assertion. The failure is logical, not a detail of which queue order AC -3 uses.

IC 29 · Remove an allowed pair with no third-variable extension

Original path-consistency problem.

Let X,Y,Z be Boolean, with X=Y, Y=Z and X≠Z. Show that binary arcs are consistent but path consistency can remove every allowed X,Y pair.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation
