Equality supports each value by itself, and inequality supports it by its complement, so every directed binary arc has a witness. For path consistency, consider an allowed pair on X=Y. Pair (0,0) requires Z=0 under Y=Z but Z=1 under X≠Z. No single Z supports both requirements, so the pair is removed. Pair (1,1) similarly requires both Z=1 and Z=0 and is removed.

The effective X,Y relation becomes empty. That is a joint-pair failure, which a relation-filtering algorithm can then propagate to domains or use directly to report inconsistency. It does not follow from merely intersecting X's and Y's domains, both of which originally contain two values. The stronger algorithm changes a relation table as well as, potentially, unary domains.

All three constraints are needed for the contradiction. Testing X=Y and Y=Z alone allows the all-zero and all-one solutions; testing the third separately supplies supports that are incompatible with those joint extensions. The pair-support table shows precisely the two contradictory requirements on Z, rather than treating three unrelated successful edge tests as a joint solution.

IC 30 · Count attacking pairs, not conflicting queens

Original min-conflicts calculation.

On a four-column board, queen rows are (1,1,3,4). Count attacking pairs. If only Q1 may change, compute the conflict count for each row choice and state every best one-variable move.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Initially the attacking pairs are ( Q1, Q2) in the same row, ( Q1, Q3) and ( Q1, Q4) on diagonals, and ( Q3, Q4) on a diagonal. The other two pairs do not attack, so the score is four. This counts constraints, not four queens or a double count of both directed pair orders.

The Q3, Q4 conflict is unaffected by moving Q1 and always contributes one. With Q1=1, its own three attacking pairs remain, totaling four. With Q1=2, it attacks Q2 diagonally but neither Q3 nor Q4, totaling two with the unaffected pair. With Q1=3, only its same-row attack on Q3 remains, again totaling two. With Q1=4, it shares a row with Q4, also totaling two. Thus rows two, three and four tie as best local moves.

None gives a zero-conflict solution because Q3, Q4 still attack. A complete tie rule must decide which move the implementation chooses. One locally best move is not a certificate of global optimality or unsatisfiability.

IC 31 · Finite assignments do not rule out a plateau cycle

Original termination problem.

Two Boolean variables have an objective that is identically one for all four assignments. A coordinate-update method changes a selected variable to another maximizing value whenever possible. Does finiteness prove termination? Give a repair and its limitation.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Every value of every variable is maximizing because the score never changes. An implementation can alternate X=0 and X=1 forever while leaving Y fixed. It visits only two of the four states, so having finitely many assignments does not prevent an infinite revisit cycle. Nondecreasing objective values are not strictly increasing objective values.

One repair is to retain the current value on equal scores and stop after a full sweep with no strict improvement. In a finite state space, strict improvements cannot continue indefinitely because only finitely many objective values exist. This establishes termination under that policy. It does not establish global optimality for a nonconstant objective: a state can have no improving one-variable neighbor while a distant assignment scores better. Another policy may allow a bounded number of sideways moves or random restarts, but its stopping and completeness properties require separate analysis. A lecture statement about convergence must identify the actual tie/stopping convention rather than infer it merely from a finite number of states.

IC 32 · A partial product need not upper-bound a completion

Original weighted-factor branch-and-bound problem.

A partial assignment has evaluated-factor product two. The best complete assignment seen so far has weight five. One unevaluated factor can reach ten. Is pruning on 2<5 sound? Derive a valid crude bound and state when the partial product itself is an upper bound.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Pruning is unsound: a completion attaining the remaining factor ten would have weight 2·10=20, exceeding the current best five. The partial product omits factors whose scope is not yet fully instantiated; it is not automatically a bound in the maximization direction.

If each unevaluated nonnegative factor has a valid upper bound uj over all completions still permitted by the branch, then U=2∏juj upper-bounds every completed product. Shared variables can prevent all individual maxima from being simultaneously attainable, making U loose, but not too small. Prune only when that valid upper bound cannot improve the incumbent, with tie handling matched to whether all optima are requested.

If every remaining factor is at most one, multiplying them cannot increase a nonnegative product, so the partial product is itself an upper bound. A factor greater than one invalidates that shortcut. Taking logs also needs care: zero factors have logarithm minus infinity and cannot be silently treated as ordinary finite costs.

IC 33 · The written voting factor graph

Adapted from Stanford CS 221 Spring 2026, Definitions, voting example.

Three variables choose B or R. Factors are [X1=B], [X1=X2], [X2=X3]+2 and [X3=R]+1. Compute every positive-weight complete assignment and identify the optimum.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

The first factor forces X1=B for any positive weight. The second then forces X2=B. Every assignment violating either condition has product zero regardless of the remaining factors. Only X3 remains free.

For (B,B,B), the factors are 1,1,3,1 and their product is three. For (B,B,R), they are 1,1,2,2 and the product is four. Thus the only positive-weight assignments are these two, with unique optimum (B,B,R). The third factor's preference for agreeing with X2 is outweighed by the fourth factor's preference for red: local preferences must be combined rather than optimized independently.

The factors are nonnegative scores and were not specified as probabilities. No normalization is needed to compare their products, but calling four a probability would be invalid. If the task were plain feasibility, either positive assignment would suffice. For maximum weight, returning the first feasible (B,B,B) without a bound or exhaustive continuation would give the wrong answer.

IC 34 · A narrow beam can discard the only solution

Original counterexample to completeness of approximate search.

Boolean X,Y have unary weight f(X)=3 for X=0 and 2 for X=1. Their only allowed binary tuple is (1,0). Use variable order X then Y and beam width one, ranking partial products without lookahead. Compare with beam width two.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

At depth one, the binary factor is not fully instantiated, so partial weights are three for X=0 and two for X=1. Width-one selection keeps X=0 and discards X=1. At the next depth, both Y values violate the binary relation, so the retained branch has no feasible completion. The algorithm reports failure even though (1,0) is a valid solution of weight two.

With width two, both depth-one assignments survive. At depth two, the only positive candidate is (1,0), which is retained and returned. This example specifies that no AC preprocessing or lookahead was used; full AC would have removed X=0 earlier and would change the trace. Approximate algorithms must be compared under their declared filtering assumptions.

The counterexample establishes that beam failure is not an unsatisfiability certificate and that a small beam lacks the complete backtracking guarantee. Increasing the width can help, but a finite width smaller than an entire frontier still does not supply a universal correctness theorem or approximation ratio.

IC 35 · A zero unaffected factor breaks a strict-improvement claim

Original coordinate-ascent boundary problem.

A weighted factor product contains f(Y)=0 at the current fixed Y and g(X), with g(0)=1 and g(1)=9. Does changing X from zero to one strictly improve the complete objective? Explain the usual locality shortcut's missing hypothesis.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Both full products are zero: 0·1=0 and 0·9=0. The local factor involving X increases, but the complete objective does not. Hence a statement that maximizing just the changed factors strictly improves the full product is false when the omitted common factor is zero.

If the product C of all unaffected factors is strictly positive, comparing Cg(a) is equivalent to comparing g(a), and strict local improvements remain strict globally. If C=0, all these coordinate choices tie in full objective. A solver may still deliberately choose the locally larger factor to seek later escape, but it must not claim a strict global ascent certificate or use that claim as its termination proof.

With nonnegative factors, omitting a nonnegative common constant cannot reverse an ordering; the issue at zero is loss of strictness and inability to infer global progress. A repair strategy for feasibility may instead minimize the number of violated hard constraints, but that is a different objective whose properties must be stated.

IC 36 · Merge explanations before the next backjump

Adapted from MIT 16.410 Lecture 7 a, PDF pages 13–17; notation and reasoning independently reconstructed.

A dead variable 6 has conflict set {4,1,0}. Variable 4 currently has conflict set {2,0}. Index 0 is a termination sentinel. Give the deepest-conflict jump, the merged set at 4 and the next jump if 4 is exhausted too. Explain why a static neighbor list is insufficient.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

The deepest actual prior decision in Conf(6) is 4, so jump from 6 to 4 and undo intervening decisions 5 and 6. Transfer the older causes of the exhausted branch to 4: Conf(4)←Conf(4)∪(Conf(6)∖{4}). The result is {2,0}∪{1,0}={2,1,0}. If every remaining value at 4 then fails with this accumulated explanation, the next deepest decision is 2, so the next jump is 4→2.

Index 0 is not a real variable to assign; it represents no earlier decision/termination in this convention. Reasons must justify rejection of every exhausted candidate, and the merge preserves earlier assumptions needed for that explanation. Omitting 1 could lead the next failure handling to forget an actual cause.

Static graph adjacency describes possible direct constraints, whereas propagation or earlier backjumps can introduce explanations involving nonadjacent decisions. A full FC/MAC backjumping implementation must track those reasons explicitly; the ordinary binary laboratory does not claim to implement this conflict-directed extension.

IC 37 · A branch deletion is not a global learned fact

Original learning-soundness problem.

Boolean X,Y satisfy equality. In branch X=1, propagation deletes Y=0. May the solver permanently delete Y=0 from the original problem? Give a valid learned relation and explain the distinction.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Permanent deletion is unsound because (X,Y)= (0,0) is a valid original solution. The deletion was justified only under X=1. On returning to the root and trying X=0, Y=0 must be available again.

A valid global nogood is the incompatible partial assignment X=1, Y=0. Its negation, “ X≠1 or Y≠0,” is implied by the original equality relation. The full original relation also excludes X=0, Y=1. Either logical consequence preserves both legitimate equal assignments. In contrast, deleting Y=0 unconditionally imposes a stronger restriction not implied by the original system.

The distinction is between a conditional inference and a theorem about every solution. Recording an explanation with its assumptions allows safe learning; keeping only the deleted value loses the condition that made the inference true. A trail restores temporary changes, while a learned constraint may survive restoration only if its global logical validity has been established. Neither mechanism can be replaced by a list of values that happened to fail in some prior branch.

IC 38 · Derive the coarser repeated-sweep bound

Course-derived complexity comparison, MIT 16.410 Lecture 6, PDF pages 4–7.

AC -1 repeatedly sweeps every directed arc until no domain changes. For n variables, e directed arcs and largest domain d, derive a naive upper bound and compare the reason for AC -3's tighter worklist bound.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

One sweep revises all e arcs, each at O(d2) naive pair-check cost, so a sweep costs O(ed2). Every nonfinal changed sweep deletes at least one value. At most nd values can be deleted from the starting domains. Allowing a final unchanged sweep gives O(nd+1) sweeps and time O(ed2(nd+1)), commonly written O(end3) for nondegenerate n, d≥1. An immediate wipeout return can reduce this count.

AC -3 does not rescan every arc after an unrelated deletion. It schedules an arc when its supporting head domain changes, charging at most O(d) revisions to that arc. This yields O(ed3) under the chapter's directed-arc and constant-lookup contract. The improvement comes from selective dependency tracking, not from making a single REVISE operation asymptotically cheaper.

Both are solution-preserving filters and both can miss the unsatisfiability of an arc-consistent odd cycle. The complexity comparison concerns reaching local consistency, not solving arbitrary CSPs in polynomial time. Initial isolated empty domains still require a separate guard.

IC 39 · Copying domains and trailing have different storage costs

Original implementation-analysis problem.

At each depth of a depth-n binary CSP search, a simple implementation copies all n domains of size at most d. Compare its worst path storage with a deletion trail, and separate teaching traces and stored solutions from solver state.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

One full domain copy costs O(nd) values. If a recursive path retains one such copy at each of O(n) levels, domain snapshots alone can occupy O(n2d) space. This is safe for rollback but not the lean O(nd) domain-state bound sometimes quoted for a single propagation invocation.

A trail shares one current domain state and records deletions with branch markers. Along one descending branch, a given original variable-value pair can be deleted at most once before restoration, so at most O(nd) such live deletion records are needed, plus recursion/assignment bookkeeping. The implementation must actually restore records in reverse to their markers; the bound does not excuse missing rollback information or mishandled support caches.

If the program stores every visual snapshot or collects exponentially many complete solutions, output storage can dominate either bound. A streaming first-solution solver, a solution enumerator and a teaching recorder therefore have different total memory use. Counts should specify whether relation-table input, temporary queues, recursion and accumulated output are included.

IC 40 · The heuristic can cost more than the next branch

Original heuristic-cost derivation.

A selected variable has at most d candidate values and δ unassigned neighbors, each with at most d values. With constant-time binary lookup, derive the cost of one-step deleted-value LCV for all candidates. Contrast trial-MAC LCV.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

For one candidate a, inspect each neighbor value b and test the relation with the now-singleton a. There are at most δd such tests, giving O(δd) cost for that candidate. Evaluating every one of at most d candidates gives O(δd2), before ordering their scores. Sorting all scores can add O(dlogd), or a first-choice scan can simply select a minimum without constructing a complete sorted list.

Trial-MAC LCV runs an entire propagation invocation for each candidate, potentially costing O(ed3) per candidate with a naive AC -3 implementation, hence O(ed4) as a coarse all-candidate bound. Domain copying/restoration and score computation add their own costs. Incremental caching can improve particular implementations but must preserve correct branch state.

Thus “LCV improves search” is a heuristic expectation, not a theorem that its overhead always pays off. State whether the score counts one-step deletions, full propagation deletions or something else; these policies can choose different orders as well as incur different costs.

IC 41 · Constraint lookup is a model assumption

Original representation-cost problem.

Compare a hashed explicit binary relation table with a predicate whose evaluation scans a length-L list. How do the REVISE and AC -3 costs change? What cost is hidden by calling the constraint constant time?

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

A naive revision can test up to d2 candidate pairs. With expected constant-time hash membership, its expected lookup work is O(d2), while storing a dense explicit table can cost O(d2) pairs per edge. A deterministic constant-time membership representation such as an indexed Boolean matrix has the same pair-count bound with its stated indexing/input-size assumptions.

If each predicate call scans L items, the same revision instead costs O(Ld2). Combining with O(ed) revisions gives O(eLd3) predicate work for AC -3. Building the tables or compiling/indexing the predicates is separate preprocessing and may itself require significant time or memory.

The number of relation tests and the cost per test are different quantities. A teaching trace can count exact tests independently of runtime. It must not silently use an expensive arithmetic, graph or scheduling oracle inside each test while claiming a whole-algorithm constant-cost bound. Input representation also matters when a higher-arity table has exponentially many tuples.

IC 42 · A failed branch with solutions elsewhere

Original fully specified counterexample used to check the authentic AC -3 scope question.

Boolean X,Y,Z satisfy relations RXY=RXZ={(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)} and Y≠Z. Show the initial CSP is arc consistent, explain failure under X=0 and enumerate the original solutions.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Initially X=0 has support zero at either neighbor, and X=1 has both supports. Each neighbor value has support X=1; zero also has support X=0. The Y,Z inequality supplies opposite-value supports. Thus all six directed arcs are consistent on full domains.

In branch X=0, the two X relations force Y=0 and Z=0. The inequality edge then has no valid pair, and MAC detects a wipeout. That proves no complete solution extends X=0.

If X=1, both neighbor domains remain Boolean until their inequality is applied. The allowed completions are (Y,Z)= (0,1) and (1,0). Therefore the original solutions are precisely (1,0,1) and (1,1,0). They verify that an intermediate branch failure cannot be promoted to a statement that the root CSP has no solution. Conversely, the initial nonempty arc-consistent domains did not imply that the branch X=0 would be extendible. Both distractor directions confuse a local statement's scope.

IC 43 · Solve through a component product, not an average

Original application of independence and counting.

One independent CSP component has four complete solutions. Another is a three-variable three-color inequality path. A third component has a single fixed compatible variable. Find the total solution count. If a new edge links the first two components, may the product rule still be used unchanged?

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

The path has 3·2·2=12 solutions, as each selected parent color permits two different child colors. The fixed-variable component contributes exactly one. With no cross constraints, every combination of component assignments is valid and every full solution decomposes uniquely, giving 4·12·1=48.

A new linking edge can forbid some of those combinations. The unconditional product rule then no longer applies. One can condition on the linked endpoint values and sum products of conditional counts, or treat the connected union as one problem. Even if the new edge happens to be redundant for the particular solution sets, that fact must be proved; graph connectivity changes invalidate an automatic independence assumption.

Counting alternatives by adding four and twelve would count assignments for only one component at a time, leaving other variables unspecified. Averaging component counts has no solution-set interpretation. The multiplicative formula follows from a Cartesian-product bijection, which is the fact to check before applying it.

IC 44 · Color symmetry needs uniform interchangeable colors

Original symmetry-breaking problem.

A three-color triangle has no unary restrictions. If A is fixed to red, count the remaining solutions and recover the original count by symmetry. Give a unary restriction that makes blindly fixing A to red unsound for existence.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Once A is red, B and C must use the two other colors in different orders, giving two solutions. Because the original constraints distinguish only equality/inequality and every vertex initially has the same three-color palette, relabeling colors is a bijection between solutions with A red, A green and A blue. These three disjoint classes have equal size, so the original count is 3·2=6.

Now impose the unary condition A=green. The restricted original CSP still has two solutions, with B,C red/blue in either order. Fixing A red makes it impossible and destroys every solution. Color names are no longer interchangeable under the unary domain specification.

Symmetry breaking is justified by an actual solution-preserving orbit argument, not by a diagram looking symmetric or colors seeming arbitrary. For counting, one must also know orbit/class sizes; removing symmetric representatives without correct multiplicities can give a wrong total even when existence is preserved.

IC 45 · The gallery capacity constraint is essential

Adapted from Stanford CS 221 Spring 2026, Examples, sculpture-gallery prompt.

Three sculptures A,B,C use rooms one or two. A and B must occupy different rooms, B and C the same room, and room two can hold at most one sculpture. Find every assignment and explain the role of the capacity constraint.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Equality B=C puts those two sculptures together. They cannot both use room two because that would place two sculptures in a room of capacity one. Thus B=C=1. The inequality A≠B then forces A=2. The assignment (A,B,C)= (2,1,1) satisfies the capacity and both relational conditions, so it is a solution and the deductions show it is unique.

If capacity were omitted, the additional assignment (1,2,2) would satisfy A≠B and B=C. It is precisely the globally invalid capacity use that the missing condition must reject. Since B=C is already known, one can derive a unary restriction B≠2, but that is an inference from both equality and capacity, not an original independent domain fact.

In a general scheduling model the capacity constraint may have higher arity or be represented by several smaller restrictions. Either encoding must preserve the original allowed complete assignments. Do not silently count a locally consistent equality pair as a valid room allocation without checking the room's occupancy limit.

IC 46 · Verify equivalent scheduling encodings by a bijection

Adapted application of Stanford's two event-scheduling formulations; numerical data are original.

Event P may use slots one or two, event Q slots two or three, and a slot holds at most one event. Enumerate event-variable solutions. Express the corresponding slot-variable assignments with an empty marker.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Event-variable domains are DP={1,2}, DQ={2,3}, with P≠Q. Their four initial pairs are (1,2), (1,3), (2,2), (2,3); only the equal-slot pair is forbidden. Thus there are three schedules.

In slot variables (S1,S2,S3), those schedules become respectively (P,Q,∅), (P,∅,Q) and (∅,P,Q). Require each event to occur exactly once, each slot to name at most one event, and event-slot eligibility. Then every valid event assignment determines exactly one slot assignment and vice versa, establishing a bijection and the same count.

If “each event exactly once” were weakened to “at most once,” the all-empty slot assignment would be admitted although both events must be scheduled. Conversely omitting the empty marker would force every slot occupied by some event and would make three slots incompatible with just two once-only events. Equivalent models need all occupancy semantics, not just similarly named variables.

IC 47 · Verification searches for a counterexample

Adapted from Stanford CS 221 Spring 2026, Examples, program-verification prompt.

Over exact real arithmetic, a program sets a=x2, b=a+y2, c=b-2xy and returns c. Encode a counterexample to c≥0 as a constraint problem, then decide it mathematically. State the arithmetic boundary.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Use variables x,y,a,b,c, constraints a=x2, b=a+y2, c=b-2xy and the negated specification c<0. A satisfying assignment would describe a valid program execution whose output violates the requested property. Substituting the first three equations gives c=x2+y2-2xy=(x-y)2, which is nonnegative over the reals. Hence the counterexample constraints are unsatisfiable, proving the specification under that exact-real model.

This is not a finite binary domain problem, so the chapter's laboratory does not claim to decide it by AC -3. The proof uses algebraic reasoning. Also, source-language assignment and mathematical equality are different operations: the constraints check consistency of a whole execution tuple and need not be evaluated in program order.

Finite-width floating-point evaluation, overflow, NaNs or other language-specific semantics require a different formal model. The exact-real identity alone is not a certificate for every machine implementation. Tests of finitely many inputs likewise do not establish the universal exact-real assertion, whereas the displayed algebraic proof does.

IC 48 · A cached support must still be alive

Original incremental-support implementation problem.

Let DX={1,2}, DY={a,b} and relation R={(1,a),(2,b)}. A solver caches support a for X=1. Another propagation removes a from Y. What must the solver do, and what goes wrong if it trusts the stale cache?

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Before using the cached witness, test that a is still in the current Y domain and that the pair remains allowed. It is no longer alive. Search for a replacement support for X=1 among the remaining domain {b}; pair (1,b) is absent, so X=1 must be removed. X=2 still has support b and remains. The resulting single pair (2,b) is the only complete solution under the new restriction.

A stale-cache shortcut would retain X=1 even though the declared arc-consistency condition fails. Caching can save repeated searches but cannot redefine what counts as a support. Backtracking adds the opposite issue: restored values or support counts must correspond to the restored branch, so a cache update policy needs a clear lifetime/validation contract.

The example uses symbolic a,b conceptually; a finite integer-coded implementation can preserve the same table with an explicit legend. The correctness obligation is membership in the current domain and relation, not whether the candidate once served as a witness earlier in the search.

IC 49 · Count cycle colorings with a two-state recurrence

Original hard mathematical transfer.

Derive the number of proper d-colorings of a labeled cycle of length k≥3. Specialize to d=3, k=4 and to d=2 with odd/even k. Explain why domain sizes alone miss the answer.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Fix the first vertex color. Let am count proper colorings of a path of m vertices whose last color equals the first, and bm those whose last color differs. Initially a1=1 and b1=0. To append a vertex, a previous different last color has exactly one choice returning to the first color, so am+1=bm. A previous equal last color has d-1 different choices; a previous different one has d-2 choices staying different from the first. Hence bm+1=(d-1)am+(d-2)bm.

The total path count for a fixed first color is am+bm=(d-1)m-1, because every appended vertex has exactly d-1 choices. Substituting am=(d-1)m-1-bm into the second recurrence gives bm+1=(d-1)m-bm. Its base value is zero. Suppose the claimed formula holds at m; then

bm+1=(d-1)m-(d-1)m+(-1)m(d-1)d=(d-1)m+1+(-1)m+1(d-1)d.

The formula also gives b1=0, completing induction for d≥2. The closing cycle edge requires the last color differ from the first, so the total cycle count is dbk=(d-1)k+(-1)k(d-1). For three colors on a four-cycle this is 16+2=18. For two colors it is 1+(-1)k, zero for odd k and two for even k.

For d=1 every cycle with an edge has zero solutions, handled directly. The identical one-vertex domain size d does not encode the parity/joint closing-edge restriction, explaining AC's limitations on the two-color examples.

IC 50 · Prove the greatest closure instead of guessing it

Original advanced fixed-point proof.

A fair AC procedure processes existing arcs and deletes only unsupported tail values until full closure, without stopping early on a wipeout. Show its final domain family contains every arc-consistent subfamily of the original domains. Deduce schedule independence, and explain the early-failure qualification.

Read the complete mathematical derivation and interpretation

Let E be any arc-consistent family contained in the initial domains. Initially every E value is present. Assume this remains true just before deleting a from the current tail domain Di. If a belonged to Ei, arc consistency of E would provide a compatible b in Ej. By induction b is still in the current head domain, contradicting the claim that a has no support. Thus a is not in Ei, and every deletion preserves the containment E⊆D.

At full fair closure, the resulting D* is itself arc consistent, because any head-domain change that could invalidate an earlier arc is eventually reconsidered. The containment proof shows E⊆D* for every initially contained arc-consistent E. Therefore D* is the greatest such family. Two fair full-closure runs each produce that greatest family, so their final domains coincide.

An implementation that stops immediately at the first empty domain returns a valid failure certificate but may leave other domains only partly filtered. Different schedules can then show different intermediate failure snapshots; those snapshots are not both claimed greatest closures. Boolean failure status and the entire returned domain vector have different reproducibility guarantees.

Four original MS examination questions, with source qualifications

Translations preserve the original choices. Answers are independently derived; no official answer key was verified. No doctoral CSP item was verified in the bounded archive pass.

MS_CE_1404_Q75 · Exact arc-consistency propagation and support witnesses

Original pinned PDF, booklet 335 C, page 18. Independent answer; official key unverified.

A CSP has variables X,Y,Z,W, with D(X)= {1,2,3}, D(Y)= {1,2,3,4}, D(Z)= {1,2,3}, and D(W)= {2,3}. Its constraints are X≠Y, Z=W, X + W≤4, and Z≠3. Which updated domains result after applying arc consistency?

  1. DX={1,2}; DY={1,2,3}; DZ={2}; DW={2}
  2. DX={1,2}; DY={1,2,3,4}; DZ={2}; DW={2}
  3. DX={1,2,3}; DY={1,2,3,4}; DZ={2}; DW={2}
  4. DX={1,2,3}; DY={2,3,4}; DZ={1,2}; DW={2}
Read all steps, distractor checks and original-wording qualifications

Step 1. First apply the unary constraint Z≠3, obtaining D(Z)= {1,2}. Unary filtering is node consistency; it must precede, or be included in, the propagation process.

Step 2. Under Z=W, Z=1 has no supporting W because W has only 2 and 3. Delete Z=1. Conversely W=3 has no supporting Z after the unary deletion, so delete W=3. Thus Z=W=2.

Step 3. Under X+ W≤4 and W=2, X=3 has no support because 3+ 2=5>4. Both X=1 and X=2 retain the support W=2. Therefore D(X)= {1,2}.

Step 4. For X≠Y, Y=1 has support X=2; Y=2 has support X=1; and each of Y=3,4 has support X=1 or 2. Thus no Y value is removed. In particular Y=4 is not constrained by X+ W≤4: that relation has scope (X,W), not (X,Y).

Step 5. All remaining directed arcs have support: each X has a distinct Y, every Y has a distinct X, X+ 2≤4 for both X values, W=2 has an X support, and equality is satisfied by Z=W=2. This is a fixed point, not just one incomplete pass.

Step 6. The six complete solutions are (X,Y,Z,W)= (1,2,2,2), (1,3,2,2), (1,4,2,2), (2,1,2,2), (2,3,2,2), (2,4,2,2). These provide an independent completeness check for the surviving values in this particular instance; in general arc consistency alone is not a global solution test.

Derived selection: option 2. This is an independent derivation, not a verified official key.

MS_CE_1404_Q73 · Residual degree, MRV and the role of LCV

Original pinned PDF, booklet 335 C, page 17. Independent answer; official key unverified.

In the illustrated map-coloring CSP, regions D and E have already been colored D=yellow and E=red. Which statement is correct?

  1. The degree heuristic selects A, B, or C as the next variable, with no preference among them.
  2. The MRV heuristic selects B or C as the next variable, with no preference between them.
  3. The degree heuristic selects A as the next variable.
  4. The LCV heuristic selects A as the next variable.
Read all steps, distractor checks and original-wording qualifications

Step 1. Translate the map into the exact adjacency graph. A borders B,C,D,E; B borders A,C,E; C borders A,B,D; D borders A,C,E; E borders A,B,D. D and E are already assigned.

Step 2. The usual degree heuristic for selecting the next variable counts constraints on other unassigned variables. The remaining graph on A,B,C is a triangle. Each of A,B,C has exactly two unassigned neighbors, so degree alone leaves a three-way tie. This proves option 1.

Step 3. Counting original graph degrees instead would give A degree 4 and B,C degree 3, but those totals include constraints to already assigned variables. That is the distractor behind option 3; it is not the residual-degree rule used to break search ties.

Step 4. Under the usual three-color palette {red,yellow,green}, constraints from D=yellow and E=red leave A={green}, B={yellow,green}, C={red,green}. Thus MRV would select A, not B or C. More generally, with a common palette of k≥3 containing these two distinct colors, A has k -2 remaining values, while B and C have k -1. The printed stem does not explicitly specify palette size; the correct degree answer does not depend on fixing it to exactly 3.

Step 5. LCV ranks candidate values after a variable has been selected; by itself it does not select a variable named A. Option 4 confuses variable ordering with value ordering.

Step 6. If three colors are used, A=green forces B=yellow and C=red, consistent with all eight edges and fixed D,E. This final coloring is a teaching check, not an additional fact printed in the question.

Derived selection: option 1. This is an independent derivation, not a verified official key.

MS_CE_1402_Q74 · AC -3 at backtracking nodes: branch scope and work bounds

Original pinned PDF, booklet 934 C, page 15. Independent answer; official key unverified.

A CSP is solved by backtracking search, with AC -3 executed at every search node. Which statement is correct?

  1. If at some stage one variable has an empty set of allowed values, the CSP has no solution.
  2. During one AC -3 execution, every edge of the constraint graph is processed at most d times, where d is the size of the variable domains.
  3. If at some stage all variables have nonempty allowed-value sets, the CSP certainly has a solution.
  4. If an allowed value is removed from a variable by AC -3, the final search answer will certainly assign that value to that variable.
Read all steps, distractor checks and original-wording qualifications

Step 1. Fix one directed arc (Xi,Xj). It is initially queued once. Later it is queued when D(Xj) shrinks, because Xi values may have lost their support in Xj. Domain values are deleted and never restored during one AC -3 invocation.

Step 2. If D(Xj) initially has at most d values, it can shrink at most d -1 times while remaining nonempty. A final deletion to the empty set stops the invocation immediately in the usual algorithm. Thus (Xi,Xj) is processed at most 1+(d -1)=d times before successful termination; failing runs cannot add another successful continuation. This is the intended statement in option 2.

Step 3. The count is per AC -3 invocation, not across all nodes of backtracking, where domains are restored and many invocations occur. With e binary undirected edges there are 2 e directed arcs; each REVISE scans at most d^2 pairs, leading to the usual O(ed3) naive upper bound.

Step 4. Option 1 incorrectly promotes a current-branch contradiction to an assertion about the original CSP. A domain wipeout means no solution extends the assignments at this node; backtracking can still find a solution in another branch.

Step 5. A fully specified example demonstrates that scope distinction. Let X,Y,Z have domains {0,1}. Let Rxy={ (0,0), (1,0), (1,1) }, Rxz={ (0,0), (1,0), (1,1) }, and require Y≠Z. The initial CSP is arc consistent. Under branch X=0, propagation forces Y=Z=0 and then produces a wipeout. Nevertheless (X,Y,Z)= (1,0,1) and (1,1,0) solve the original CSP.

Step 6. Option 3 is false: a triangle of pairwise inequality constraints with every domain {0,1} is arc consistent, since either value has the opposite value as support on each edge; yet the triangle cannot be two-colored.

Step 7. Option 4 reverses the meaning of sound deletion. A removed value cannot participate in any complete solution extending the current branch. It is not a promised eventual assignment; after backtracking restores domains, a value may be available in another branch, but that is a different local problem.

Direction qualification. The intended choice is 2 under the usual directed-arc convention. If an undirected edge counts both orientations together, the exact numerical bound is 2 d, not d. The source wording alone must not hide that distinction.

Source qualification. The work-bound statement uses the standard directed-arc AC -3 interpretation, with initial domain size at most d and one initial copy of each directed arc. An undirected edge represents two directed arcs, giving at most 2 d total directed revisions rather than literally d for both directions combined. The printed Persian says graph edge; the customary textbook interpretation is an arc. The empty-domain conclusion must be scoped to the current backtracking node.

Derived selection: option 2. This is an independent derivation, not a verified official key.

MS_CE_1405_Q74 · Tree-CSP reverse arc-consistency complexity

Original pinned PDF, booklet 135 A, page 15. Independent answer; official key unverified.

When solving a CSP by performing the arc-consistency check in reverse order, with n variables each able to take d values, what is the time order of the complete algorithm?

  1. O(nd)
  2. O(nd)
  3. O(n+d)
  4. O(nd2)
Read all steps, distractor checks and original-wording qualifications

Step 1. Under the standard intended tree-CSP interpretation, root the constraint tree and choose an order in which each parent precedes its children. There are n -1 edges.

Step 2. Process each nonroot variable in reverse order, revising the arc from its parent to that child. A parent value must have at least one supporting child value. At most d parent values are compared with at most d child values, so one revision costs O(d2). Over n -1 edges this is O(nd2).

Step 3. The reverse-order sweep establishes directional consistency. If the root domain remains nonempty, choose a root value and assign each child a compatible value in the forward order. The retained parent values have supports, and disjoint subtrees have no cross-edge constraints, so no backtracking is necessary.

Step 4. With naive support scanning, forward assignment costs at most O(nd), and constructing the order costs O(n). Consequently O(n) + O(nd2) + O(nd) = O(nd2), matching option 4.

Step 5. The structural condition matters. A cyclic graph can be arc consistent while unsatisfiable, as shown by the two-color triangle; one reverse sweep does not make arbitrary CSPs solvable in this polynomial time. This authentic item should therefore be introduced as an explicitly qualified tree-CSP question rather than evidence for a general complexity claim.

Source qualification. The printed stem does not explicitly state that the constraint graph is a tree. Its phrase reverse-order arc consistency invokes the standard tree-structured CSP algorithm. O(nd2) is valid under that intended structural premise, not for a general cyclic CSP. Preserve this qualification in the chapter instead of silently adding a tree premise to the source translation.

Derived selection: option 4. This is an independent derivation, not a verified official key.

27. Complete summary and final examination decisions

Synthesis: what each layer actually proves

A model defines the problem: variables name choices, domains name permitted values, and relations specify jointly legal tuples. A complete solution must satisfy every original relation. A locally consistent partial assignment has passed only the fully instantiated constraints; it may have no completion. Binary support filtering removes a tail value only when no compatible head value remains. That deletion is sound because any putative solution containing the tail value would itself have supplied a head witness.

AC -3 manages dependencies between these tests. A head-domain change can invalidate incoming supports, so affected arcs return to the queue. Within one invocation, domains only shrink and finitely many values can disappear. A successful fixed point certifies local support, not a joint solution. A wipeout refutes the current branch; it refutes the original problem only when its assumptions are the root conditions, or when a complete surrounding search exhausts every alternative.

Backtracking obtains completeness by eventually trying every necessary candidate under exact rollback. MRV, residual degree and LCV order that work; they are not independent logical pruning rules. MAC combines sound support filtering with complete branching. Tree structure allows a stronger polynomial construction because separately supported child subtrees do not share cross constraints. Conditioning on a supplied cycle cutset recovers that structure at an exponential cost in the cutset size. Global constraints and stronger consistency enforce genuinely joint witnesses that separate pairwise tests may miss. Local repair and narrow beams can be effective, but their unsuccessful termination does not certify impossibility.

Use the following decisions after the full lesson. Each includes a condition or reason so that it can be transferred to a new problem rather than memorized as an isolated slogan.

Modeling and counting

  1. Name the requested object before counting. Complete assignments, distinct partial maps, action-order paths, tree nodes and relation tests are different sets; a count for one does not answer a question about another.
  2. Count independent choices only before imposing their coupling constraints. Uniform domains give dn complete tuples, but that is generally an upper bound on solutions, not the number of solutions.
  3. Charge the permutation factor only when assignment order is an action choice. Allowing all variable orders produces n!dn complete paths; selecting one next variable at each state removes this particular redundancy.
  4. Use the partial-map count for arbitrary scopes. Each variable is absent or has one of d values, giving (1+d)n distinct partial assignments; a fixed-order tree visits only prefix scopes.
  5. Include internal nodes when asked for the whole tree. Its unconstrained fixed-order size is ∑k=0ndk; for d=1 this is n+1, so a geometric-series division by d-1 must be avoided.
  6. Treat a domain as a set rather than an interval. Filtering can leave holes, and replacing a set by its minimum–maximum interval silently restores forbidden values.
  7. Distinguish local legality from extendibility. Satisfying all currently instantiated constraints does not prove that the remaining variables can be assigned.
  8. Check occupancy in alternative encodings. At-most-one queen or event restrictions permit empty arrangements unless exactly-one requirements are supplied.
  9. Conjoin predicates on the same pair when joint pair support is claimed. A witness for equality and another for inequality cannot satisfy their conjunction.
  10. Transpose an asymmetric relation on a reversed arc. Filtering Y against X under X<Y checks the original allowed pairs in reversed coordinate order; it does not add Y<X.
  11. Retain higher-arity information explicitly. Pairwise projections of even parity are unrestricted and therefore do not reconstruct the original triple relation.
  12. Account for an auxiliary tuple domain. Hidden-variable conversion is exact, but an arity-k relation can require dk tuple states and is not automatically a compact encoding.

Branching and heuristics

  1. Specify the problem's stopping rule. One verified solution solves feasibility, whereas counting all solutions or proving a weighted optimum requires continued work or a valid certificate.
  2. Restore every temporary deletion before a sibling branch. A contradiction under X=1 does not justify carrying its empty domains into X=0.
  3. Separate assignments from singleton domains. Filtering can force a value without increasing recursive assignment depth; traces must identify which record they describe.
  4. Apply MRV to current legal possibilities. Raw initial sizes can be misleading after earlier assignments unless legal values are recomputed or maintained.
  5. Use residual degree only at its declared priority. A high-degree variable does not override a strictly smaller domain under MRV-first ordering.
  6. Count unassigned neighbors for the usual degree tie-break. Already assigned neighbors explain existing restrictions but do not count as remaining search connections.
  7. State a final tie rule when reproducing a trace. Alphabetical or declared input order makes tied MRV/degree decisions deterministic; the heuristic names alone may not.
  8. Keep variable selection separate from value ordering. MRV and degree choose a variable; LCV ranks its candidate values and does not independently select a variable.
  9. Define what an LCV score counts. Deleting three values in one neighbor and deleting one in each of two neighbors reverse the rankings of deleted-value and affected-neighbor policies.
  10. Do not turn an ordering score into an elimination proof. A poorly ranked value can still be the only path to a solution and must remain available in a complete search.
  11. Include heuristic overhead in a cost comparison. One-step LCV over all d candidates costs O(δd2) relation tests; trial propagation can be substantially more expensive.
  12. Qualify symmetry breaking by an actual invariance. Fixing a triangle's first color is safe under interchangeable palettes, but a unary color requirement can destroy that symmetry.

Propagation and work bounds

  1. Write the arc direction before deleting values. In X→Y, only X is revised and Y supplies witnesses; interchanging those roles changes the intermediate trace.
  2. Use the correct quantifier order. Each tail value needs some compatible head value; all tail values need not share the same witness.
  3. Apply unary restrictions as well as binary propagation. In the authentic numeric question, removing Z=3 is essential before equality can force Z=W=2.
  4. Check isolated empty domains explicitly. Such a variable never appears in the queue but still makes the CSP impossible.
  5. Requeue only existing incoming arcs after a shrink. The neighbors of the changed variable may have lost support; unrelated nonedges do not become constraints.
  6. Justify the skipped immediate reverse arc. A value removed for having no support could not have been supporting any surviving value on the transposed same relation; this proof relies on the representation contract.
  7. Distinguish a popped arc from a full propagation invocation. One REVISE costs at most O(d2) naive checks; the worklist can revisit it after later head-domain changes.
  8. Charge repeated processing to strict head shrinkage. With one initial copy and immediate wipeout return, a directed arc is revised at most d times in one invocation.
  9. Declare whether e counts directed arcs or undirected edges. Each undirected binary edge supplies two directions; asymptotic order may agree while an exact numerical bound differs by two.
  10. State the relation-lookup assumption. The O(ed3) bound counts constant-cost pair tests; an oracle costing L per test changes the corresponding work to O(eLd3).
  11. Do not reuse the invocation bound for the whole search. Restoring domains at many backtracking nodes permits many separate AC -3 runs and exponential total work.
  12. Distinguish forward checking from propagated closure. After A=0 in A=B=C, one layer reduces B, while MAC also carries that consequence to C.
  13. Use the singleton-head cost when it is actually present. Assigned-value forward checking scans at most δd candidate pairs, unlike a generic arbitrary-domain revision.
  14. Interpret a nonempty AC fixed point as necessary local evidence. A two-color odd cycle supplies a direct counterexample to treating it as a solution certificate.
  15. Scope a wipeout to its assumptions. A branch can fail while another branch solves the original CSP; the authentic work-bound question explicitly tests this distinction.
  16. Separate full-closure uniqueness from failure snapshots. Fair complete filtering has a greatest fixed domain family, but immediate failure can stop before other domains reach that closure.
  17. Validate cached witnesses against current domains. A value that once supported a candidate cannot continue to justify it after that witness is deleted.
  18. Count trace storage separately from solver storage. Recording every before/after state or collecting every solution can dominate the live domains, queue and recursion memory.

Structure and stronger consistency

  1. Prove the tree premise before invoking the tree algorithm. A single reverse sweep plus forward witness selection is complete on a tree; cycles can carry incompatible joint requirements.
  2. Revise parents against children in reverse order. Child subtrees must already support their surviving values when those values are used to justify a parent.
  3. Check every root or isolated component for emptiness. A forest is not automatically satisfiable; each component must pass its own domain and support checks.
  4. Explain why forward tree choices do not collide. Different child subtrees have no cross edges, so choosing a support in one does not invalidate a sibling subtree.
  5. Separate tree existence from tree counting. A witness constructs one solution; counting requires sums over compatible child choices and products over independent child subtrees.
  6. Include exact-integer costs when counts are large. The usual O(nd2) message count measures arithmetic operations, not an unconditional unit-cost bound on arbitrarily large integers.
  7. Verify that a supplied cutset really leaves a forest. Removing one vertex from K4 leaves a triangle; two vertices are needed for a cycle cutset.
  8. Check internal and boundary constraints in every cutset branch. A residual tree does not excuse an already invalid cutset assignment or a missing constraint to an assigned vertex.
  9. Retain enumeration cost when the residual graph is empty. Setting c=n does not make solving cost zero; up to dn complete cutset assignments still require verification.
  10. Do not charge cutset discovery to an algorithm that assumes it is given. Finding a good cutset and exploiting a supplied one are separate computational tasks.
  11. Ask whether witnesses must be jointly compatible. Pairwise inequality can support Z=1 separately against X and Y while global all-different has no joint tuple containing Z=1.
  12. Use Hall's condition on subsets, not just total counts. Any subset with too few available values disproves a complete distinct-value allocation, even when every binary arc has support.
  13. Distinguish bare k-consistency from strong k-consistency. A universal extension claim can be vacuous when no lower-order consistent assignment exists; the constructive theorem requires all lower levels and a nonempty unary base.
  14. Recognize that path consistency filters pairs. Removing a pair with no joint third-variable extension is stronger than merely deleting unsupported individual domain values.

Learning, repair and weighted objectives

  1. Preserve antecedents when learning from a branch. Equality under X=1 excludes the pair ( X=1, Y=0), not the original value Y=0 in every branch.
  2. Merge all necessary causes when backjumping. An explanation for one failed candidate does not explain exhaustion of all candidates; earlier causes must survive the conflict-set union.
  3. Do not interpret failed local repair as an impossibility proof. Min-conflicts can plateau or cycle, and a finite unsuccessful run does not exhaust the complete assignment space.
  4. Require a tie/stopping policy in a convergence argument. Strict improvement in a finite state space terminates, whereas arbitrary equal-score moves can revisit states forever.
  5. Distinguish feasibility from maximum weight. A positive product satisfies all hard zero/nonzero restrictions, but another positive assignment can have a larger product.
  6. Use a valid upper bound before pruning a weighted branch. A partial product can increase after a remaining factor greater than one; multiply by justified remaining-factor bounds instead.
  7. Do not infer strict global ascent after omitting a zero constant. Improving changed factors leaves a full product zero when an unaffected factor is zero.
  8. State beam-search completeness and cost assumptions. A narrow beam can discard the only solution; O(nKd) assumes bounded incremental scoring and linear selection, and excludes other representation costs.

Final answer protocol

For a new question, write its variables, exact domains and original scopes first. State any branch, palette, tree, lookup or queue assumptions before calculating. Show the mathematical operation that changes a domain, count or bound, then verify the proposed result against the original model. If the original wording omits a necessary premise, identify the intended interpretation and its limit explicitly. A complete solution should teach why the answer follows and why its tempting alternatives fail.
